```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
  dev = "png", dpi = 200, fig.retina = 1,
  fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 3
)

# ---- palette and plot scaffolding --------------------------------------------

blue   <- "#3f77b1"
orange <- "#dd7a35"
slate  <- "#5e6878"
red    <- "#b23a48"
light  <- "#b1b8bf"
gridc  <- "#ececec"

fig_par <- function() {
  par(mar = c(3.1, 3.6, 0.6, 0.8), mgp = c(2.1, 0.55, 0), las = 1,
      tcl = -0.3, cex.axis = 0.8, cex.lab = 0.85, bty = "l")
}

# Empty plot with light gridlines, left/bottom axes only.
# Pass xat + xlabels for a categorical x-axis.
fig_frame <- function(xlim, ylim, xlab, ylab, yat = pretty(ylim),
                      xat = NULL, xlabels = NULL) {
  fig_par()
  plot(NA, xlim = xlim, ylim = ylim, xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab,
       axes = FALSE, xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
  abline(h = yat, col = gridc, lwd = 0.8)
  if (is.null(xlabels)) {
    xt <- pretty(xlim)
    abline(v = xt, col = gridc, lwd = 0.8)
    axis(1, at = xt, lwd = 0, lwd.ticks = 1)
  } else {
    abline(v = xat, col = gridc, lwd = 0.8)
    axis(1, at = xat, labels = xlabels, lwd = 0, lwd.ticks = 1)
  }
  axis(2, at = yat, lwd = 0, lwd.ticks = 1)
  box(bty = "l")
}

dot <- function(x, y, col, cex = 1.5) {
  points(x, y, pch = 21, bg = col, col = "white", cex = cex, lwd = 1.2)
}

legend_tl <- function(labels, cols, lty = 1, lwd = 3, pch = NA, pt.bg = NA) {
  legend("topleft", legend = labels, col = cols, lty = lty, lwd = lwd,
         pch = pch, pt.bg = pt.bg, bty = "n", cex = 0.75, seg.len = 1.6,
         inset = c(0.01, 0.02))
}

# Two categories joined by one line per group (2 x 2 designs).
two_by_two <- function(xlabels, xlab, ylim, series, cols) {
  fig_frame(c(0.6, 2.4), ylim, xlab, "Outcome", yat = seq(ylim[1], ylim[2], 5),
            xat = 1:2, xlabels = xlabels)
  for (i in seq_along(series)) {
    lines(1:2, series[[i]], col = cols[i], lwd = 3)
    dot(1:2, series[[i]], cols[i], cex = 1.3)
  }
  legend_tl(names(series), cols)
}

# ---- one function per figure -------------------------------------------------

fig_01a <- function() {
  set.seed(609)
  y <- 74 + as.vector(scale(rnorm(24))) * 5
  x <- runif(24, 0.65, 1.35)
  fig_frame(c(0.2, 2.6), c(55, 90), "", "Score", yat = seq(55, 90, 5),
            xat = 1, xlabels = "Sample")
  abline(h = 70, col = slate, lty = 2, lwd = 2)
  points(x, y, pch = 16, col = adjustcolor(blue, 0.45), cex = 0.9)
  segments(0.6, 74, 1.4, 74, col = blue, lwd = 3)
  text(1.47, 74, "Sample mean 74", adj = 0, cex = 0.75, col = blue, font = 2)
  text(2.55, 70, "Benchmark 70", adj = c(1, 1.5), cex = 0.75, col = slate)
}

fig_01b <- function() {
  set.seed(610)
  yc <- 50 + as.vector(scale(rnorm(18))) * 5
  yt <- 62 + as.vector(scale(rnorm(18))) * 5
  fig_frame(c(0.4, 2.6), c(35, 80), "Group (different people)", "Score",
            yat = seq(35, 80, 5), xat = 1:2, xlabels = c("Control", "Treatment"))
  points(runif(18, 0.8, 1.2), yc, pch = 16, col = adjustcolor(blue, 0.45), cex = 0.9)
  points(runif(18, 1.8, 2.2), yt, pch = 16, col = adjustcolor(orange, 0.5), cex = 0.9)
  segments(0.72, 50, 1.28, 50, col = blue, lwd = 3)
  segments(1.72, 62, 2.28, 62, col = orange, lwd = 3)
  text(1.3, 50, "mean 50", adj = 0, cex = 0.75, col = blue, font = 2)
  text(2.3, 62, "mean 62", adj = 0, cex = 0.75, col = orange, font = 2)
}

fig_01c <- function() {
  pre  <- c(A = 50, B = 60, C = 55)
  post <- c(A = 58, B = 66, C = 62)
  fig_frame(c(0.5, 2.7), c(45, 70), "Period (same people measured twice)", "Score",
            yat = seq(45, 70, 5), xat = 1:2, xlabels = c("Pre", "Post"))
  segments(1, pre, 2, post, col = light, lwd = 2)
  dot(rep(1, 3), pre, slate, cex = 1.1)
  dot(rep(2, 3), post, slate, cex = 1.1)
  text(2.06, post, paste0(names(post), ": +", post - pre), adj = 0, cex = 0.72, col = slate)
  dot(1, 55, blue)
  dot(2, 62, orange)
  text(0.94, 55, "Pre mean 55", adj = 1, cex = 0.75, col = blue, font = 2)
  text(2.06, 69, "Post mean 62", adj = 0, cex = 0.75, col = orange, font = 2)
  segments(2, 62, 2.05, 68.2, col = orange, lwd = 1)
}

fig_02 <- function() {
  m <- c(70, 76, 61)
  cols <- c(blue, orange, slate)
  fig_frame(c(0.4, 3.6), c(50, 85), "Program", "Mean score", yat = seq(50, 85, 5),
            xat = 1:3, xlabels = c("Traditional", "Hybrid", "Online"))
  dot(1:3, m, cols, cex = 1.7)
  text(1:3, m + 2.4, m, cex = 0.8, col = cols, font = 2)
}

fig_03 <- function() {
  fig_frame(c(0, 10), c(10, 70), "X", "Outcome", yat = seq(10, 70, 10))
  abline(20, 3, col = blue, lwd = 3)
  abline(30, 3, col = orange, lwd = 3)
  legend_tl(c("A", "B"), c(blue, orange))
}

fig_04 <- function() {
  fig_frame(c(0, 10), c(10, 90), "X", "Outcome", yat = seq(10, 90, 10))
  abline(20, 2, col = blue, lwd = 3)
  abline(30, 5, col = orange, lwd = 3)
  legend_tl(c("A", "B"), c(blue, orange))
}

fig_05 <- function() {
  two_by_two(c("Low resources", "High resources"), "Setting", c(30, 75),
             list(Control = c(40, 60), Program = c(55, 60)), c(blue, orange))
}

fig_06 <- function() {
  two_by_two(c("Pre", "Post"), "Period", c(40, 80),
             list(Control = c(50, 55), Treatment = c(50, 70)), c(blue, orange))
}

fig_07 <- function() {
  y <- c(20, 25, 30)
  cols <- c(slate, blue, orange)
  fig_frame(c(-0.5, 2.5), c(15, 35), "Doses received", "Mean outcome",
            yat = seq(15, 35, 5), xat = 0:2, xlabels = c("0", "1", "2"))
  lines(0:2, y, col = light, lwd = 2)
  dot(0:2, y, cols, cex = 1.7)
  text(0:2, y + 1.8, y, cex = 0.8, col = cols, font = 2)
  text(c(0.5, 1.5), c(22.5, 27.5), "+5", adj = c(-0.3, 1.6), cex = 0.75, col = slate)
}

fig_08 <- function() {
  fig_frame(c(-6, 6), c(5, 60), "Time relative to intervention", "Outcome",
            yat = seq(10, 60, 10))
  abline(v = 0, col = slate, lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
  segments(-1, 18, 5, 30, col = light, lty = 3, lwd = 2)
  segments(-5, 10, -1, 18, col = blue, lwd = 3)
  segments(0, 30, 5, 55, col = orange, lwd = 3)
  dot(-1, 18, blue)
  dot(0, 30, orange)
  legend_tl(c("Before", "After", "Pre-trend extended"), c(blue, orange, light),
            lty = c(1, 1, 3), lwd = c(3, 3, 2))
}

fig_09 <- function() {
  fig_frame(c(-5, 5), c(25, 75), "Running variable minus cutoff", "Outcome",
            yat = seq(30, 70, 10))
  abline(v = 0, col = slate, lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
  segments(-5, 30, 0, 40, col = blue, lwd = 3)
  segments(0, 50, 5, 70, col = orange, lwd = 3)
  dot(0, 40, blue)
  dot(0, 50, orange)
  legend_tl(c("Below", "Above"), c(blue, orange))
}

fig_10 <- function() {
  set.seed(1010)
  x  <- runif(70, 1, 9)
  y  <- 10 + 4 * x + rnorm(70, 0, 3)
  y0 <- 30 + rnorm(16, 0, 2.5)
  fig_frame(c(-0.8, 10), c(0, 55), "Fundraising expense", "Donations",
            yat = seq(0, 50, 10))
  abline(v = 0, col = slate, lty = 3, lwd = 1.5)
  points(x, y, pch = 16, col = adjustcolor(blue, 0.5), cex = 0.8)
  segments(0, 10, 9, 46, col = blue, lwd = 3)
  points(rep(0, 16), y0, pch = 16, col = adjustcolor(orange, 0.7), cex = 0.9)
}

fig_11 <- function() {
  set.seed(1111)
  xs <- runif(35, 1, 9); ys <- 10 + 3 * xs + rnorm(35, 0, 2.5)
  xl <- runif(35, 1, 9); yl <- 17 + 5 * xl + rnorm(35, 0, 2.5)
  y0 <- 30 + rnorm(16, 0, 2.5)
  fig_frame(c(-0.8, 10), c(0, 75), "Fundraising expense", "Donations",
            yat = seq(0, 70, 10))
  points(xs, ys, pch = 16, col = adjustcolor(blue, 0.45), cex = 0.8)
  points(xl, yl, pch = 16, col = adjustcolor(orange, 0.45), cex = 0.8)
  segments(0, 10, 9, 37, col = blue, lwd = 3)
  segments(0, 17, 9, 62, col = orange, lwd = 3)
  points(rep(0, 16), y0, pch = 16, col = adjustcolor(slate, 0.7), cex = 0.9)
  legend_tl(c("Small", "Large", "Zero X"), c(blue, orange, slate),
            lty = c(1, 1, NA), lwd = c(3, 3, NA), pch = c(NA, NA, 16))
}

# One panel of the single-outlier figure: Y = t for 2010-2020 (t = 1..11), except
# that `odd_year` is 10 units too high. The line is the OLS fit with no dummy.
outlier_panel <- function(odd_year, label) {
  year <- 2010:2020
  y <- year - 2009
  y[year == odd_year] <- y[year == odd_year] + 10
  fig_frame(c(2009.3, 2020.7), c(-5, 25), "Year", "Outcome", yat = seq(-5, 25, 5),
            xat = seq(2010, 2020, 2), xlabels = seq(2010, 2020, 2))
  fit <- lm(y ~ year)
  clip(2009.3, 2020.7, -5, 25)
  abline(fit, col = orange, lwd = 2.5)
  dot(year[year != odd_year], y[year != odd_year], blue, cex = 1.2)
  dot(odd_year, y[year == odd_year], red, cex = 1.5)
  mtext(label, side = 3, line = -1.1, adj = 0.04, cex = 0.72, font = 2, col = slate)
}

fig_12 <- function() {
  op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2)); on.exit(par(op))
  outlier_panel(2015, "A: odd year 2015")
  outlier_panel(2020, "B: odd year 2020")
}

covid_base <- function(ylim) {
  fig_frame(c(2013.5, 2027.8), ylim, "Year", "Outcome", yat = seq(ylim[1] + 5, ylim[2], 10),
            xat = seq(2014, 2026, 2), xlabels = seq(2014, 2026, 2))
  rect(2019.6, ylim[1], 2022.4, ylim[2], col = adjustcolor(slate, 0.1), border = NA)
}

covid_legend <- function(first = "Pre-COVID trend, extended", extra = NULL, extra_col = NULL) {
  legend_tl(c(first, "Anomaly years", "Stable post period", extra),
            c(blue, slate, orange, extra_col), lty = c(2, NA, 1, rep(1, length(extra))),
            lwd = c(2, NA, 3, rep(3, length(extra))), pch = c(NA, 16, NA, rep(NA, length(extra))))
}

# 13A: flat before and after, no shift
fig_13a <- function() {
  covid_base(c(35, 80))
  segments(2014, 60, 2027, 60, col = blue, lty = 2, lwd = 2)
  dot(2014:2019, rep(60, 6), blue, cex = 1.2)
  dot(2020:2022, c(44, 42, 53), slate, cex = 1.3)
  lines(2023:2027, rep(60, 5), col = orange, lwd = 3)
  dot(2023:2027, rep(60, 5), orange, cex = 1.2)
  covid_legend("Pre-COVID level, extended")
}

# 13B and 13C: rising trend, post level 9 above it
covid_trend <- function(ylim) {
  covid_base(ylim)
  segments(2014, 50, 2027, 76, col = blue, lty = 2, lwd = 2)
  dot(2014:2019, 50 + 2 * (0:5), blue, cex = 1.2)
  dot(2020:2022, c(44, 42, 53), slate, cex = 1.3)
  lines(2023:2027, 77 + 2 * (0:4), col = orange, lwd = 3)
  dot(2023:2027, 77 + 2 * (0:4), orange, cex = 1.2)
}

fig_13b <- function() {
  covid_trend(c(35, 90))
  covid_legend()
}

fig_13c <- function() {
  covid_trend(c(35, 100))
  lines(c(2023, 2027), c(77, 93), col = red, lwd = 3)
  covid_legend(extra = "Alternative: steeper post slope", extra_col = red)
}

fig_14 <- function() {
  two_by_two(c("Pre", "Post"), "Period", c(40, 80),
             list(A = c(50, 55), B = c(50, 70)), c(blue, orange))
}
```

```{=html}
<div class="wrap">

  <header class="masthead">
    <p class="eyebrow">Unit 14 &middot; Practicing Dummy Variable Specifications</p>
    <h1>Build the Model from the Hypothesis</h1>
    <p class="dek">Dummy variables, reference categories, interactions, and structural changes. Fourteen
      exercises that start from a picture and a question, and end with a single coefficient that answers
      it.</p>
    <nav class="jump" aria-label="Sections">
      <a href="#how">How to use</a>
      <a href="#questions">Questions</a>
      <a href="#solutions">Solutions</a>
      <a href="#synthesis">Synthesis</a>
    </nav>
  </header>

  <!-- ================================================================== -->
  <section id="how">
    <div class="sec-head">
      <p class="num">Section one</p>
      <h2>How to use this handout</h2>
      <p class="sub">The conventions, the four-step routine, and the one rule that answers most of the
        questions.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="concepts">
      <p class="panel-label">Before you start</p>

      <p class="claim">Every picture is a set of conditional means.</p>
      <p>Points and lines stand for group means or conditional means, not fitted estimates with standard
        errors. <strong>The picture suggests a contrast; it does not establish statistical significance or
        causality.</strong> A real test needs case-level data and a standard error appropriate to the
        design. The numbers are illustrative.</p>

      <p class="claim">Four steps for every question.</p>
      <ol>
        <li><strong>Define the indicators</strong> and name the reference (omitted) group.</li>
        <li><strong>Write the regression equation.</strong> Assume an error term in every model.</li>
        <li><strong>State the null hypothesis</strong> as a restriction on a coefficient, such as
          <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub> = 0</span>.</li>
        <li><strong>Interpret each relevant coefficient</strong> as a specific difference between two
          points in the picture.</li>
      </ol>

      <p class="claim">The one rule behind almost every answer.</p>
      <p>Software tests every coefficient against zero. A coefficient on a dummy is
        <strong>the gap between that category and the omitted category, measured where every other
        predictor equals zero</strong>. So if you want a contrast tested for you, choose two things:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>the <strong>reference category</strong>, so the comparison is against the group you care
          about; and</li>
        <li>the <strong>zero point</strong> of any continuous variable (by centering), so the gap is
          measured where you care about it: a cutoff, an intervention date, a benchmark.</li>
      </ul>

      <p class="claim">How to get coefficients from a picture.</p>
      <p>Write the equation once for each cell, setting each dummy to its 0/1 value. The reference cell
        gives you the intercept. Every other cell adds exactly one new coefficient, so you can solve for
        each one by subtraction.</p>

      <p class="claim">Coding conventions.</p>
      <ul>
        <li>Every indicator is written <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>name</sub></span> and equals 1 when the
          name is true.</li>
        <li>The column headed <span class="m">1</span> is the intercept. <span class="m"><i>Y</i></span> is
          the illustrated cell mean unless stated otherwise.</li>
        <li>Design matrices often display <em>complementary</em> indicators side by side (for example
          <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>treat</sub></span> and <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>control</sub></span>)
          so you can see both reference choices. <strong>Never enter a complete set of complementary
          indicators together with an intercept.</strong> Columns left out of the model are shown in grey.</li>
        <li>Rows are observation <em>types</em>. Real data would have many rows of each type, which is
          where the standard errors come from.</li>
      </ul>

      <p class="claim">Work the questions before reading the solutions.</p>
      <p>Each solution repeats the figure and question, then gives a short answer, the reasoning, a design
        matrix, the model, a coefficient table, and a common mistake.</p>
    </div>
  </section>

  <!-- ================================================================== -->
```

```{=html}
        regression that tests whether the population mean equals 70. What does its intercept measure? Would a
        group dummy help?</p></div>

      <div class="callout">
        <span class="lbl">Short answer</span>
        <p>Subtract the benchmark from the outcome, <span class="m"><i>Y</i><sub>c</sub> = <i>Y</i> &minus; 70</span>,
          and regress it on a constant alone. The intercept is the sample mean minus the benchmark
          (<span class="m">74 &minus; 70 = 4</span>), and testing <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>0</sub> = 0</span>
          is exactly the one-sample t-test of <span class="m"><i>μ</i> = 70</span>. A group dummy cannot help:
          there is only one group, so the dummy would be a column of ones that duplicates the intercept.</p>
      </div>

      <h4>Why this works</h4>
      <p>A regression with nothing but a constant estimates the mean of the outcome, and its standard error is
        <span class="m"><i>s</i>/&radic;<i>n</i></span>, the same standard error the one-sample t-test uses. The
        only problem is that software tests the intercept against <em>zero</em>, and nobody doubts that the
        mean score is above zero. Shifting the outcome by 70 moves the benchmark to zero, so the default test
        becomes the test you want.</p>
      <p>An equivalent route is to regress raw <span class="m"><i>Y</i></span> on a constant
        (<span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>0</sub> = 74</span>) and ask for the linear-hypothesis test
        <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>0</sub> = 70</span>. The t-statistic is identical. Recentering simply makes
        the right test the default one.</p>

      <h4>Design matrix</h4>
      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="dm">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Observation type</th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>Y</i></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>Y</i><sub>c</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m">1</span></th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><th scope="row">Sample mean</th><td>74</td><td class="y">4</td><td>1</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>
      <p>In real data each person supplies one row with their own <span class="m"><i>Y</i><sub>c</sub></span>.</p>

      <h4>Model</h4>
      <div class="eq"><span class="m"><i>Y</i><sub>c</sub> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>ε</i></span></div>

      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="coef">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Coefficient</th><th scope="col">Value</th><th scope="col">Testing it equals zero asks&hellip;</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>4</td><td>Does the population mean equal the benchmark of 70?</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="mistake">
        <span class="lbl">Common mistakes</span>
        <ul>
          <li><strong>Creating <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>above</sub> = I(<i>Y</i> &gt; 70)</span> as a
            predictor.</strong> It is built from the outcome itself, so it only splits cases into above and below
            the benchmark. It says nothing about whether the <em>mean</em> equals 70.</li>
          <li><strong>Regressing raw <span class="m"><i>Y</i></span> on a constant and reading the default
            p-value.</strong> That tests whether the mean is zero, not whether it is 70.</li>
        </ul>
      </div>
      <a class="to-sol" href="#q1a">&larr; Back to question</a>
    </article>

    <!-- 1B ------------------------------------------------------------ -->
    <article class="ex" id="s1b">
      <h3>1B. Two independent samples</h3>
      <figure class="fig">
```

```{r s01b, fig.alt="Control scores centred on 50 and treatment scores centred on 62, in two separate groups."}
fig_01b()
```

```{=html}
      </figure>
      <div class="prompt"><p>Independent control and treatment groups have means 50 and 62. Code one dummy so its
        coefficient tests their difference. What changes if treatment is omitted instead?</p></div>

      <div class="callout">
        <span class="lbl">Short answer</span>
        <p>Use <span class="m"><i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>d</i><sub>treat</sub> + <i>ε</i></span>.
          The intercept is the control mean (50) and <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>1</sub> = 12</span> is
          treatment minus control, so testing <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>1</sub> = 0</span> is the two-sample
          t-test. Omitting treatment instead gives <span class="m">(62, &minus;12)</span>: the same test, the same
          |t|, with the sign reversed.</p>
      </div>

      <h4>Why this works</h4>
      <p>With one dummy and a constant, the constant takes care of the omitted group and the dummy measures how
        far the other group sits from it. Write the equation for each row:</p>
      <ul class="cells">
        <li>Control (<span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>treat</sub> = 0</span>): <span class="m"><i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> = 50</span></li>
        <li>Treatment (<span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>treat</sub> = 1</span>): <span class="m"><i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub> = 62</span>, so <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>1</sub> = 12</span></li>
      </ul>
      <p>Ordinary OLS standard errors pool the two groups&rsquo; variances, so this matches the equal-variance
        (Student) t-test. For the Welch test, ask for heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors.</p>

      <h4>Design matrix</h4>
      <p>Both indicators are shown so you can see both reference choices. Include only <strong>one</strong>
        alongside the intercept.</p>
      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="dm">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Observation type</th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>Y</i></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m">1</span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>treat</sub></span></th><th scope="col" class="off"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>control</sub></span></th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><th scope="row">Control</th><td class="y">50</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td class="off">1</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Treatment</th><td class="y">62</td><td>1</td><td>1</td><td class="off">0</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <h4>Models</h4>
      <div class="eq"><span class="m">Model A (control reference): <i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>d</i><sub>treat</sub> + <i>ε</i></span></div>
      <div class="eq"><span class="m">Model B (treatment reference): <i>Y</i> = <i>γ</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>γ</i><sub>1</sub><i>d</i><sub>control</sub> + <i>ε</i></span></div>

      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="coef">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Coefficient</th><th scope="col">Value</th><th scope="col">Testing it equals zero asks&hellip;</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">Model A &middot; control reference</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>50</td><td>Is the control mean zero? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>12</td><td>Does the treatment mean equal the control mean?</td></tr>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">Model B &middot; treatment reference</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>62</td><td>Is the treatment mean zero? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>&minus;12</td><td>Does the control mean equal the treatment mean?</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="mistake">
        <span class="lbl">Common mistakes</span>
        <ul>
          <li><strong>Entering <span class="m">1</span>, <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>treat</sub></span>, and
            <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>control</sub></span> together.</strong> Because
            <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>treat</sub> + <i>d</i><sub>control</sub> = 1</span> on every row, the
            two dummies add up to the intercept column (perfect collinearity), and the coefficients cannot be
            identified.</li>
          <li><strong>Calling <span class="m"><i>γ</i><sub>1</sub></span> &ldquo;treatment minus
            control.&rdquo;</strong> In Model B it is control minus treatment. The named category is always
            compared <em>to</em> the omitted one.</li>
        </ul>
      </div>
      <a class="to-sol" href="#q1b">&larr; Back to question</a>
    </article>

    <!-- 1C ------------------------------------------------------------ -->
    <article class="ex" id="s1c">
      <h3>1C. Paired samples</h3>
      <figure class="fig">
```

```{r s01c, fig.alt="Three people measured before and after: A from 50 to 58, B from 60 to 66, C from 55 to 62. Pre mean 55, post mean 62."}
fig_01c()
```

```{=html}
      </figure>
      <div class="prompt"><p>The <em>same</em> people A, B, and C are measured before and after a program.
        Construct (a) a regression on within-person differences, (b) a long-format model with
        <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>A</sub>, <i>d</i><sub>B</sub>, <i>d</i><sub>C</sub></span> and
        <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span>, and (c) the equivalent model with a person-specific
        intercept <span class="m"><i>α</i><sub><i>i</i></sub></span>. Why does treating the two periods as
        independent samples give a different standard error?</p></div>

      <div class="callout">
        <span class="lbl">Short answer</span>
        <p>All three models estimate the same thing: the average within-person change,
          <span class="m">(8 + 6 + 7)/3 = 7</span>, with the same standard error. The independent-samples
          version gets the same 7 but a much larger standard error, because it leaves the stable differences
          <em>between</em> people in the error term. Pairing makes each person their own control.</p>
      </div>

      <h4>(a) Difference-score regression</h4>
      <p>Compute each person&rsquo;s change, <span class="m">Δ<sub>A</sub> = 8, Δ<sub>B</sub> = 6,
        Δ<sub>C</sub> = 7</span>, and regress it on a constant:</p>
      <div class="eq"><span class="m">Δ<sub><i>i</i></sub> = <i>γ</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>u</i><sub><i>i</i></sub>,&ensp; <i>γ̂</i><sub>0</sub> = 7</span></div>
      <p>This is 1A again, applied to the differences. Testing <span class="m"><i>γ</i><sub>0</sub> = 0</span>
        is the paired t-test.</p>

      <h4>(b) Long format with ID dummies</h4>
      <div class="eq"><span class="m"><i>Y</i><sub><i>it</i></sub> = <i>α</i><sub>A</sub><i>d</i><sub>A</sub> + <i>α</i><sub>B</sub><i>d</i><sub>B</sub> + <i>α</i><sub>C</sub><i>d</i><sub>C</sub> + <i>β</i><i>d</i><sub>post</sub> + <i>ε</i><sub><i>it</i></sub></span></div>
      <p>There is <strong>no common intercept</strong>: all three ID dummies are included, and together they do
        the intercept&rsquo;s job. Each person gets their own baseline, and <span class="m"><i>β̂</i> = 7</span> is
        the common within-person change.</p>
      <p>Why are the fitted intercepts <span class="m">50.5, 59.5, 55</span> rather than the observed pre scores
        <span class="m">50, 60, 55</span>? The model forces everyone to share one change of 7, but the actual
        changes are 8, 6, and 7. Each <span class="m"><i>α̂</i><sub><i>i</i></sub></span> therefore lands at
        the person&rsquo;s own average minus half the common change. For A, <span class="m">54 &minus; 3.5 = 50.5</span>.
        The leftover &plusmn;0.5 residuals are the only error the model sees.</p>

      <h4>(c) Person-specific intercepts</h4>
      <div class="eq"><span class="m"><i>Y</i><sub><i>it</i></sub> = <i>α</i><sub><i>i</i></sub> + <i>β</i><i>d</i><sub>post</sub> + <i>ε</i><sub><i>it</i></sub>,&ensp; <i>i</i> &isin; {A, B, C}</span></div>
      <p>This is the same model as (b) in shorter notation. <span class="m"><i>α</i><sub><i>i</i></sub></span>
        stands for the three ID columns; it is <em>not</em> a single common intercept. This is the one-way
        fixed-effects model you will see again in panel data.</p>

      <h4>Why the standard errors differ</h4>
      <p>People differ a lot in <em>level</em> (pre scores of 50, 60, 55) but very little in <em>change</em>
        (8, 6, 7). The independent-samples test compares the two columns of scores, so all of that level
        variation counts as noise. The paired test compares each person with themselves, so it disappears.</p>
      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="coef">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Analysis</th><th scope="col">Estimate</th><th scope="col">What goes into the standard error</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><td>Paired / ID dummies</td><td>7</td><td>SD of the changes = 1, so SE = <span class="m">1/&radic;3 &asymp; 0.58</span>, <span class="m"><i>t</i> &asymp; 12</span></td></tr>
            <tr><td>Independent samples</td><td>7</td><td>Pooled SD of levels &asymp; 4.5, so SE &asymp; 3.7, <span class="m"><i>t</i> &asymp; 1.9</span></td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <h4>Design matrix</h4>
      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="dm">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Observation type</th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>Y</i></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>A</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>B</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>C</sub></span></th><th scope="col" class="off"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>pre</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span></th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><th scope="row">A, pre</th><td class="y">50</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td class="off">1</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">A, post</th><td class="y">58</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td class="off">0</td><td>1</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">B, pre</th><td class="y">60</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td class="off">1</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">B, post</th><td class="y">66</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td class="off">0</td><td>1</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">C, pre</th><td class="y">55</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td class="off">1</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">C, post</th><td class="y">62</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td class="off">0</td><td>1</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="coef">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Coefficient</th><th scope="col">Value</th><th scope="col">Testing it equals zero asks&hellip;</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">ID dummies / <span class="m"><i>α</i><sub><i>i</i></sub></span></th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>α</i><sub>A</sub>, <i>α</i><sub>B</sub>, <i>α</i><sub>C</sub></td><td>50.5, 59.5, 55</td><td>Is this person&rsquo;s fitted baseline zero? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i></td><td>7</td><td>Is the average within-person change zero?</td></tr>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">Difference scores</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>7</td><td>Is the mean of the paired differences zero?</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="mistake">
        <span class="lbl">Common mistakes</span>
        <ul>
          <li><strong>Fitting <code>Y ~ d_post</code> and calling it a paired t-test.</strong> The coefficient is
            still 7 in balanced data, but the standard error treats the six rows as independent and ignores the
            matched IDs.</li>
          <li><strong>Adding a common intercept to <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>A</sub>, <i>d</i><sub>B</sub>,
            <i>d</i><sub>C</sub></span>.</strong> The ID dummies sum to one on every row, so this is perfectly
            collinear. The same goes for entering both <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>pre</sub></span> and
            <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span> alongside all the ID dummies.</li>
        </ul>
      </div>
      <a class="to-sol" href="#q1c">&larr; Back to question</a>
    </article>

    <!-- 2 ------------------------------------------------------------- -->
    <article class="ex" id="s2">
      <h3>2. Three categories, two reference choices</h3>
      <figure class="fig">
```

```{r s02, fig.alt="Mean scores: Traditional 70, Hybrid 76, Online 61."}
fig_02()
```

```{=html}
      </figure>
      <div class="prompt"><p>Means are Traditional 70, Hybrid 76, Online 61. Model A should test Hybrid versus
        Traditional and Online versus Traditional directly. Model B should test Traditional versus Online and
        Hybrid versus Online directly. Specify both and calculate the coefficients.</p></div>

      <div class="callout">
        <span class="lbl">Short answer</span>
        <p>Omit the category that every requested contrast shares. Model A omits Traditional and gives
          <span class="m">(70, 6, &minus;9)</span>. Model B omits Online and gives
          <span class="m">(61, 9, 15)</span>. The two models fit the data identically; they just put p-values
          on different comparisons.</p>
      </div>

      <h4>Why this works</h4>
      <p>Three groups allow three pairwise comparisons, but a model with an intercept has room for only two
        dummy coefficients. Whichever category you omit becomes the comparison point for <em>both</em> of them.
        The third comparison is still available as a difference of coefficients, but it needs a separate
        linear-combination test. In Model A, Hybrid versus Online is
        <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>1</sub> &minus; <i>β</i><sub>2</sub> = 6 &minus; (&minus;9) = 15</span>,
        which Model B reports directly as <span class="m"><i>γ</i><sub>2</sub></span>.</p>
      <ul class="cells">
        <li>Model A, Traditional row: <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>0</sub> = 70</span>. Hybrid:
          <span class="m">70 + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub> = 76</span>. Online: <span class="m">70 + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub> = 61</span>.</li>
        <li>Model B, Online row: <span class="m"><i>γ</i><sub>0</sub> = 61</span>. Traditional:
          <span class="m">61 + <i>γ</i><sub>1</sub> = 70</span>. Hybrid: <span class="m">61 + <i>γ</i><sub>2</sub> = 76</span>.</li>
      </ul>

      <h4>Design matrix</h4>
      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="dm">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Observation type</th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>Y</i></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m">1</span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>traditional</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>hybrid</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>online</sub></span></th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><th scope="row">Traditional</th><td class="y">70</td><td>1</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Hybrid</th><td class="y">76</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Online</th><td class="y">61</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>1</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>
      <p>Each model uses the constant and <strong>two</strong> of the three indicators.</p>

      <h4>Models</h4>
      <div class="eq"><span class="m">Model A: <i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>d</i><sub>hybrid</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub><i>d</i><sub>online</sub> + <i>ε</i></span></div>
      <div class="eq"><span class="m">Model B: <i>Y</i> = <i>γ</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>γ</i><sub>1</sub><i>d</i><sub>traditional</sub> + <i>γ</i><sub>2</sub><i>d</i><sub>hybrid</sub> + <i>ε</i></span></div>

      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="coef">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Coefficient</th><th scope="col">Value</th><th scope="col">Testing it equals zero asks&hellip;</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">Model A &middot; Traditional reference</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>70</td><td>Is the Traditional mean zero? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>6</td><td>Does Hybrid equal Traditional?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></td><td>&minus;9</td><td>Does Online equal Traditional?</td></tr>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">Model B &middot; Online reference</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>61</td><td>Is the Online mean zero? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>9</td><td>Does Traditional equal Online?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>2</sub></td><td>15</td><td>Does Hybrid equal Online?</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="mistake">
        <span class="lbl">Common mistakes</span>
        <ul>
          <li><strong>Omitting Hybrid for Model A.</strong> Both coefficients would then compare with Hybrid, and
            Online versus Traditional would be a difference of two coefficients rather than one.</li>
          <li><strong>Including all three indicators with the constant.</strong> They sum to the intercept
            column, so the model is not identified.</li>
        </ul>
      </div>
      <a class="to-sol" href="#q2">&larr; Back to question</a>
    </article>

    <!-- 3 ------------------------------------------------------------- -->
    <article class="ex" id="s3">
      <h3>3. Parallel lines: a common slope</h3>
      <figure class="fig">
```

```{r s03, fig.alt="Two parallel lines: A is 20 + 3X and B is 30 + 3X."}
fig_03()
```

```{=html}
      </figure>
      <div class="prompt"><p>Group A follows <span class="m">20 + 3<i>X</i></span> and B follows
        <span class="m">30 + 3<i>X</i></span>. Make the slope and the group gap individual coefficient tests.
        What restriction on the slopes have you imposed?</p></div>

      <div class="callout">
        <span class="lbl">Short answer</span>
        <p><span class="m"><i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>X</i> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub><i>d</i><sub>B</sub> + <i>ε</i></span>
          gives <span class="m">(20, 3, 10)</span>. <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></span> is the common
          slope and <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></span> is the vertical gap between the lines. You have
          <strong>imposed</strong> equal slopes, not tested them: with no
          <span class="m"><i>X</i>&middot;<i>d</i><sub>B</sub></span> term, the model cannot draw anything but
          parallel lines.</p>
      </div>

      <h4>Why this works</h4>
      <p>Write the line for each group:</p>
      <ul class="cells">
        <li>A (<span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>B</sub> = 0</span>): <span class="m"><i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>X</i></span></li>
        <li>B (<span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>B</sub> = 1</span>): <span class="m"><i>Y</i> = (<i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub>) + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>X</i></span></li>
      </ul>
      <p>A dummy on its own moves a line up or down. It cannot tilt it. Because both lines share
        <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></span>, the gap <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub> = 10</span>
        is the same at every value of <span class="m"><i>X</i></span>. That is the one situation in which
        &ldquo;the group difference&rdquo; has a single answer. To <em>check</em> whether the lines really are
        parallel, add the interaction and test it (exercise 4).</p>

      <h4>Design matrix</h4>
      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="dm">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Observation type</th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>Y</i></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m">1</span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>X</i></span></th><th scope="col" class="off"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>A</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>B</sub></span></th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><th scope="row">A, <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 0</span></th><td class="y">20</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td class="off">1</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">A, <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 5</span></th><td class="y">35</td><td>1</td><td>5</td><td class="off">1</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">B, <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 0</span></th><td class="y">30</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td class="off">0</td><td>1</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">B, <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 5</span></th><td class="y">45</td><td>1</td><td>5</td><td class="off">0</td><td>1</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <h4>Models</h4>
      <div class="eq"><span class="m">A reference: <i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>X</i> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub><i>d</i><sub>B</sub> + <i>ε</i></span></div>
      <div class="eq"><span class="m">B reference: <i>Y</i> = <i>γ</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>γ</i><sub>1</sub><i>X</i> + <i>γ</i><sub>2</sub><i>d</i><sub>A</sub> + <i>ε</i></span></div>

      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="coef">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Coefficient</th><th scope="col">Value</th><th scope="col">Testing it equals zero asks&hellip;</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">A reference</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>20</td><td>Is A&rsquo;s mean at <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 0</span> zero? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>3</td><td>Is the common slope zero?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></td><td>10</td><td>Are A and B equal at the same <span class="m"><i>X</i></span>?</td></tr>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">B reference</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>30</td><td>Is B&rsquo;s mean at <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 0</span> zero? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>3</td><td>Is the common slope zero?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>2</sub></td><td>&minus;10</td><td>Are A and B equal at the same <span class="m"><i>X</i></span>?</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="mistake">
        <span class="lbl">Common mistakes</span>
        <ul>
          <li><strong>Adding <span class="m"><i>X</i>&middot;<i>d</i><sub>B</sub></span> but still calling the
            <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>B</sub></span> coefficient &ldquo;the gap.&rdquo;</strong> Once the
            slopes can differ, the gap is <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub><i>X</i></span>,
            and <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></span> alone is the gap only at
            <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 0</span>.</li>
          <li><strong>Using a dummy to test a slope difference.</strong> A dummy alone can only shift intercepts.</li>
        </ul>
      </div>
      <a class="to-sol" href="#q3">&larr; Back to question</a>
    </article>

    <!-- 4 ------------------------------------------------------------- -->
    <article class="ex" id="s4">
      <h3>4. Nonparallel lines: intercept and slope interactions</h3>
      <figure class="fig">
```

```{r s04, fig.alt="Two diverging lines: A is 20 + 2X and B is 30 + 5X."}
fig_04()
```

```{=html}
      </figure>
      <div class="prompt"><p>A follows <span class="m">20 + 2<i>X</i></span> and B follows
        <span class="m">30 + 5<i>X</i></span>. Embed tests for the intercept difference, the slope difference,
        and A&rsquo;s slope. Then recode so B&rsquo;s slope is a single coefficient.</p></div>

      <div class="callout">
        <span class="lbl">Short answer</span>
        <p><span class="m"><i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>X</i> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub><i>d</i><sub>B</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub>(<i>X</i>&middot;<i>d</i><sub>B</sub>) + <i>ε</i></span>
          gives <span class="m">(20, 2, 10, 3)</span>: A&rsquo;s slope, the intercept gap, and the slope gap are
          each one coefficient. B&rsquo;s slope is <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>1</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub> = 5</span>,
          a sum. To make it a single coefficient, make B the reference by using
          <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>A</sub></span> and <span class="m"><i>X</i>&middot;<i>d</i><sub>A</sub></span>
          instead. Then <span class="m"><i>γ</i><sub>1</sub> = 5</span>.</p>
      </div>

      <h4>Why this works</h4>
      <p>Write each group&rsquo;s line and match it to the picture:</p>
      <ul class="cells">
        <li>A: <span class="m"><i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>X</i> = 20 + 2<i>X</i></span></li>
        <li>B: <span class="m"><i>Y</i> = (<i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub>) + (<i>β</i><sub>1</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub>)<i>X</i> = 30 + 5<i>X</i></span></li>
      </ul>
      <p>The main-effect dummy shifts the intercept and the interaction shifts the slope. Every coefficient
        describes the reference group (A) or B&rsquo;s <em>difference</em> from it. In particular,
        <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></span> is not &ldquo;the effect of <span class="m"><i>X</i></span>&rdquo;;
        it is the effect of <span class="m"><i>X</i></span> <strong>for A</strong>.</p>
      <p>Also note what the intercept gap means now. <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub> = 10</span> is the gap
        at <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 0</span> only. At <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 5</span> the gap is
        <span class="m">10 + 3&middot;5 = 25</span>. If <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 0</span> is outside your data or
        not meaningful, center <span class="m"><i>X</i></span> at a value you care about, and
        <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></span> becomes the gap there.</p>

      <h4>Design matrix</h4>
      <p>The interaction columns are products of <span class="m"><i>X</i></span> and the named dummy. Use the B
        pair <strong>or</strong> the A pair, depending on the reference.</p>
      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="dm">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Observation type</th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>Y</i></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m">1</span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>X</i></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>A</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>B</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>X</i><i>d</i><sub>A</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>X</i><i>d</i><sub>B</sub></span></th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><th scope="row">A, <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 0</span></th><td class="y">20</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">A, <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 5</span></th><td class="y">30</td><td>1</td><td>5</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>5</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">B, <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 0</span></th><td class="y">30</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">B, <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 5</span></th><td class="y">55</td><td>1</td><td>5</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>5</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <h4>Models</h4>
      <div class="eq"><span class="m">A reference: <i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>X</i> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub><i>d</i><sub>B</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub>(<i>X</i><i>d</i><sub>B</sub>) + <i>ε</i></span></div>
      <div class="eq"><span class="m">B reference: <i>Y</i> = <i>γ</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>γ</i><sub>1</sub><i>X</i> + <i>γ</i><sub>2</sub><i>d</i><sub>A</sub> + <i>γ</i><sub>3</sub>(<i>X</i><i>d</i><sub>A</sub>) + <i>ε</i></span></div>

      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="coef">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Coefficient</th><th scope="col">Value</th><th scope="col">Testing it equals zero asks&hellip;</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">A reference</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>20</td><td>Is A&rsquo;s intercept zero? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>2</td><td>Is A&rsquo;s slope zero?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></td><td>10</td><td>Are A and B equal at <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 0</span>?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>3</sub></td><td>3</td><td>Do A and B have the same slope?</td></tr>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">B reference</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>30</td><td>Is B&rsquo;s intercept zero? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>5</td><td>Is B&rsquo;s slope zero?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>2</sub></td><td>&minus;10</td><td>Are A and B equal at <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 0</span>?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>3</sub></td><td>&minus;3</td><td>Do A and B have the same slope?</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="mistake">
        <span class="lbl">Common mistakes</span>
        <ul>
          <li><strong>Leaving out the interaction and reading <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>B</sub></span> as a
            slope difference.</strong> Without <span class="m"><i>X</i><i>d</i><sub>B</sub></span> the model forces
            the slopes to match (exercise 3).</li>
          <li><strong>Reading <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>3</sub> = 3</span> as B&rsquo;s slope.</strong> It is
            the <em>difference</em> between B&rsquo;s slope and A&rsquo;s. B&rsquo;s slope is
            <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>1</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub></span>.</li>
        </ul>
      </div>
      <a class="to-sol" href="#q4">&larr; Back to question</a>
    </article>

    <!-- 5 ------------------------------------------------------------- -->
    <article class="ex" id="s5">
      <h3>5. A 2 &times; 2 program-by-setting design</h3>
      <figure class="fig">
```

```{r s05, fig.alt="Control rises from 40 in low-resource settings to 60 in high; program rises from 55 to 60."}
fig_05()
```

```{=html}
      </figure>
      <div class="prompt"><p>Control means are 40 (low resource) and 60 (high); program means are 55 and 60. Test
        the program effect in low settings, its effect in high settings, and whether the effects differ.
        Which reference choice makes the high-setting effect a single coefficient?</p></div>

      <div class="callout">
        <span class="lbl">Short answer</span>
        <p>With low settings as the reference (use <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>high</sub></span>), the model
          gives <span class="m">(40, 15, 20, &minus;15)</span>. The program effect in low settings is
          <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>1</sub> = 15</span>, the difference in effects is
          <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>3</sub> = &minus;15</span>, and the high-setting effect is the sum
          <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>1</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub> = 0</span>. To test the high-setting
          effect as one coefficient, make <strong>high</strong> the reference by using
          <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>low</sub></span>. Then <span class="m"><i>γ</i><sub>1</sub> = 0</span>.</p>
      </div>

      <h4>Why this works</h4>
      <p>The key idea: <strong>a main effect in an interacted model is the effect where the other dummy equals
        zero</strong>, which is in the reference category of the other factor. So the program coefficient is
        the program effect in whichever setting you omitted.</p>
      <ul class="cells">
        <li>Control, low: <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>0</sub> = 40</span></li>
        <li>Program, low: <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub> = 55 &rarr; <i>β</i><sub>1</sub> = 15</span></li>
        <li>Control, high: <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub> = 60 &rarr; <i>β</i><sub>2</sub> = 20</span></li>
        <li>Program, high: <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub> = 60 &rarr; <i>β</i><sub>3</sub> = &minus;15</span></li>
      </ul>
      <p>The interaction is the gap between what you&rsquo;d expect if program and setting simply added up
        (<span class="m">40 + 15 + 20 = 75</span>) and what you actually see (60). Here the program closes the
        resource gap in low settings and does nothing where resources are already high. The interaction test
        is the same in both codings; only its sign flips.</p>

      <h4>Design matrix</h4>
      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="dm">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Observation type</th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>Y</i></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m">1</span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>program</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>low</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>high</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>program</sub><i>d</i><sub>low</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>program</sub><i>d</i><sub>high</sub></span></th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><th scope="row">Control, low</th><td class="y">40</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Program, low</th><td class="y">55</td><td>1</td><td>1</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Control, high</th><td class="y">60</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Program, high</th><td class="y">60</td><td>1</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>1</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <h4>Models</h4>
      <div class="eq"><span class="m">Low reference: <i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>d</i><sub>program</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub><i>d</i><sub>high</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub>(<i>d</i><sub>program</sub><i>d</i><sub>high</sub>) + <i>ε</i></span></div>
      <div class="eq"><span class="m">High reference: <i>Y</i> = <i>γ</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>γ</i><sub>1</sub><i>d</i><sub>program</sub> + <i>γ</i><sub>2</sub><i>d</i><sub>low</sub> + <i>γ</i><sub>3</sub>(<i>d</i><sub>program</sub><i>d</i><sub>low</sub>) + <i>ε</i></span></div>

      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="coef">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Coefficient</th><th scope="col">Value</th><th scope="col">Testing it equals zero asks&hellip;</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">Low-setting reference</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>40</td><td>Is the control/low mean zero? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>15</td><td>Is there a program effect in low settings?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></td><td>20</td><td>Do high and low settings differ among controls?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>3</sub></td><td>&minus;15</td><td>Is the program effect the same in both settings?</td></tr>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">High-setting reference</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>60</td><td>Is the control/high mean zero? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>0</td><td>Is there a program effect in high settings?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>2</sub></td><td>&minus;20</td><td>Do low and high settings differ among controls?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>3</sub></td><td>15</td><td>Is the program effect the same in both settings?</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="mistake">
        <span class="lbl">Common mistakes</span>
        <ul>
          <li><strong>Coding <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>high</sub></span> but reading the program coefficient as
            the high-setting effect.</strong> Because <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>high</sub> = 0</span> in low
            settings, the program main effect describes <em>low</em> settings.</li>
          <li><strong>Calling <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></span> &ldquo;the average program
            effect.&rdquo;</strong> In an interacted model there is no single program effect. There is one per
            setting.</li>
          <li><strong>Entering <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>low</sub></span> and
            <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>high</sub></span> together with an intercept.</strong> That is perfectly
            collinear.</li>
        </ul>
      </div>
      <a class="to-sol" href="#q5">&larr; Back to question</a>
    </article>

    <!-- 6 ------------------------------------------------------------- -->
    <article class="ex" id="s6">
      <h3>6. Pre/post with a comparison group</h3>
      <figure class="fig">
```

```{r s06, fig.alt="Control rises from 50 to 55; treatment rises from 50 to 70."}
fig_06()
```

```{=html}
      </figure>
      <div class="prompt"><p>Control changes from 50 to 55; treatment changes from 50 to 70. Test the baseline
        group difference, the control group&rsquo;s time change, and the <em>difference in changes</em>. Which
        coefficient is the last contrast?</p></div>

      <div class="callout">
        <span class="lbl">Short answer</span>
        <p>With control/pre as the reference,
          <span class="m"><i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>d</i><sub>treat</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub><i>d</i><sub>post</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub>(<i>d</i><sub>treat</sub><i>d</i><sub>post</sub>) + <i>ε</i></span>
          gives <span class="m">(50, 0, 5, 15)</span>. <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></span> is the
          baseline gap, <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></span> is the control group&rsquo;s change, and the
          <strong>interaction <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>3</sub></span></strong> is the difference in changes.
          This is the difference-in-differences estimator.</p>
      </div>

      <h4>Why this works</h4>
      <p>This is exercise 5 with &ldquo;setting&rdquo; replaced by &ldquo;time.&rdquo; Solve cell by cell:</p>
      <ul class="cells">
        <li>Control, pre: <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>0</sub> = 50</span></li>
        <li>Treatment, pre: <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub> = 50 &rarr; <i>β</i><sub>1</sub> = 0</span></li>
        <li>Control, post: <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub> = 55 &rarr; <i>β</i><sub>2</sub> = 5</span></li>
        <li>Treatment, post: <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub> = 70 &rarr; <i>β</i><sub>3</sub> = 15</span></li>
      </ul>
      <p>So <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>3</sub> = (70 &minus; 50) &minus; (55 &minus; 50) = 20 &minus; 5 = 15</span>.
        The control group&rsquo;s change (5) is the counterfactual: what would have happened to the treatment
        group without the program. <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub> = 55</span>
        is the treatment group&rsquo;s expected post score under that counterfactual, and
        <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>3</sub></span> is how far the observed 70 sits above it. Reading
        <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>3</sub></span> as a program effect requires the
        <strong>parallel-trends</strong> assumption: without the program, both groups would have changed by the
        same amount.</p>
      <p>Changing the reference changes what the main effects mean. Flipping <em>one</em> reference (group or
        period) flips the sign of the interaction; flipping both leaves it unchanged.</p>

      <h4>Design matrix</h4>
      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="dm">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Observation type</th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>Y</i></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m">1</span></th><th scope="col" class="off"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>control</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>treat</sub></span></th><th scope="col" class="off"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>pre</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>treat</sub><i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span></th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><th scope="row">Control, pre</th><td class="y">50</td><td>1</td><td class="off">1</td><td>0</td><td class="off">1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Treatment, pre</th><td class="y">50</td><td>1</td><td class="off">0</td><td>1</td><td class="off">1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Control, post</th><td class="y">55</td><td>1</td><td class="off">1</td><td>0</td><td class="off">0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Treatment, post</th><td class="y">70</td><td>1</td><td class="off">0</td><td>1</td><td class="off">0</td><td>1</td><td>1</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="coef">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Coefficient</th><th scope="col">Value</th><th scope="col">Testing it equals zero asks&hellip;</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">Control/pre reference</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>50</td><td>Is the control pre mean zero? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>0</td><td>Are treatment and control equal at baseline?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></td><td>5</td><td>Did the control group change from pre to post?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>3</sub></td><td>15</td><td>Did the treatment group change by the same amount as control?</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="mistake">
        <span class="lbl">Common mistakes</span>
        <ul>
          <li><strong>Using the post-period group gap (<span class="m">70 &minus; 55 = 15</span>) as the
            estimator.</strong> It matches here only because the baseline gap happens to be zero. In general it
            mixes the program effect with any pre-existing difference.</li>
          <li><strong>Using the treatment group&rsquo;s own change (20).</strong> It fails to subtract the change
            of 5 that would have happened anyway.</li>
          <li><strong>Adding <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>control</sub></span> beside
            <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>treat</sub></span>, or <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>pre</sub></span>
            beside <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span>, with an intercept.</strong> Both are
            collinear.</li>
        </ul>
      </div>
      <a class="to-sol" href="#q6">&larr; Back to question</a>
    </article>

    <!-- 7 ------------------------------------------------------------- -->
    <article class="ex" id="s7">
      <h3>7. Cumulative doses</h3>
      <figure class="fig">
```

```{r s07, fig.alt="Mean outcome 20 after zero doses, 25 after one, 30 after two."}
fig_07()
```

```{=html}
      </figure>
      <div class="prompt"><p>Mean outcomes after zero, one, and two doses are 20, 25, and 30. Build
        <em>cumulative</em> indicators so each coefficient is the increment from receiving another dose.
        Compare this with indicators for exactly one and exactly two doses.</p></div>

      <div class="callout">
        <span class="lbl">Short answer</span>
        <p>Define <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>dose1</sub> = 1</span> if a person received <strong>at least</strong>
          one dose and <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>dose2</sub> = 1</span> if they received at least two. The
          model gives <span class="m">(20, 5, 5)</span>: <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></span> is the gain
          from the first dose and <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></span> is the <em>additional</em> gain
          from the second. Exact-group indicators give <span class="m">(20, 5, 10)</span> instead, comparing
          each group with zero doses.</p>
      </div>

      <h4>Why this works</h4>
      <p>A two-dose person has <em>both</em> cumulative indicators switched on, so their predicted mean is
        <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub></span>. A one-dose
        person has <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub></span>. The difference between
        them is <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></span> alone, the step from one dose to two.</p>
      <p>With exact-group indicators, a two-dose person has only <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>two</sub></span>
        switched on, so <span class="m"><i>α</i><sub>2</sub></span> is the whole distance from zero doses. The
        second increment is still there, but only as
        <span class="m"><i>α</i><sub>2</sub> &minus; <i>α</i><sub>1</sub> = 5</span>.</p>
      <p>Both codings fit the same three means; they differ only in which contrasts get a p-value. Cumulative
        coding also lets you test whether each dose adds the same amount
        (<span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>1</sub> = <i>β</i><sub>2</sub></span>). That is exactly the assumption a
        linear dose term <span class="m"><i>β</i>&middot;doses</span> would impose without testing. The same
        stacking idea reappears in exercises 8 and 13, where a post-period dummy is added on top of a trend.</p>

      <h4>Design matrix</h4>
      <p>The exact-group pair (<span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>one</sub>, <i>d</i><sub>two</sub></span>) and the
        cumulative pair (<span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>dose1</sub>, <i>d</i><sub>dose2</sub></span>) encode
        <strong>different contrasts</strong>. Use one pair, not both.</p>
      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="dm">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Observation type</th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>Y</i></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m">1</span></th><th scope="col" class="off"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>none</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>one</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>two</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>dose1</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>dose2</sub></span></th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><th scope="row">Zero doses</th><td class="y">20</td><td>1</td><td class="off">1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">One dose</th><td class="y">25</td><td>1</td><td class="off">0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Two doses</th><td class="y">30</td><td>1</td><td class="off">0</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>1</td><td>1</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <h4>Models</h4>
      <div class="eq"><span class="m">Exact groups: <i>Y</i> = <i>α</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>α</i><sub>1</sub><i>d</i><sub>one</sub> + <i>α</i><sub>2</sub><i>d</i><sub>two</sub> + <i>ε</i></span></div>
      <div class="eq"><span class="m">Cumulative: <i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>d</i><sub>dose1</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub><i>d</i><sub>dose2</sub> + <i>ε</i></span></div>

      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="coef">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Coefficient</th><th scope="col">Value</th><th scope="col">Testing it equals zero asks&hellip;</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">Exact groups</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>α</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>20</td><td>Is the zero-dose mean zero? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>α</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>5</td><td>Does one dose differ from none?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>α</i><sub>2</sub></td><td>10</td><td>Do two doses differ from none?</td></tr>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">Cumulative</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>20</td><td>Is the zero-dose mean zero? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>5</td><td>Does the first dose add anything?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></td><td>5</td><td>Does the second dose add anything beyond the first?</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="mistake">
        <span class="lbl">Common mistakes</span>
        <ul>
          <li><strong>Calling <span class="m"><i>α</i><sub>2</sub> = 10</span> &ldquo;the effect of the second
            dose.&rdquo;</strong> It is the total difference between two doses and none.</li>
          <li><strong>Coding <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>dose1</sub> = 1</span> only for people with exactly one
            dose.</strong> That turns it back into an exact-group indicator, and it no longer measures cumulative
            exposure.</li>
          <li><strong>Reading the dose coefficients causally without asking how dosage was assigned.</strong>
            People who choose a second dose may differ from those who do not.</li>
        </ul>
      </div>
      <a class="to-sol" href="#q7">&larr; Back to question</a>
    </article>

    <!-- 8 ------------------------------------------------------------- -->
    <article class="ex" id="s8">
      <h3>8. Interrupted time series</h3>
      <figure class="fig">
```

```{r s08, fig.alt="A pre-intervention line with slope 2 reaching 18 at t = -1, then a jump to 30 at t = 0 and a steeper post line with slope 5."}
fig_08()
```

```{=html}
      </figure>
      <div class="prompt"><p>Time is centered so the first post-intervention period is
        <span class="m"><i>t</i> = 0</span>. The pretrend slope is 2. At <span class="m"><i>t</i> = 0</span>
        the post line is 10 above the extrapolated pre line, and then it rises 5 per period. Specify separate
        tests for the immediate level change and the slope change. What if the graph has a kink but no
        jump?</p></div>

      <div class="callout">
        <span class="lbl">Short answer</span>
        <p><span class="m"><i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>t</i> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub><i>d</i><sub>post</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub><i>t</i><sub>after</sub> + <i>ε</i></span>,
          with <span class="m"><i>t</i><sub>after</sub> = <i>t</i>&middot;<i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span>, gives
          <span class="m">(20, 2, 10, 3)</span>. <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></span> is the immediate
          jump, <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>3</sub></span> is the change in slope, and the post slope is
          <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>1</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub> = 5</span>. A kink with no jump means
          <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub> = 0</span>. You can test that, or impose it by dropping
          <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span>.</p>
      </div>

      <h4>Why this works</h4>
      <p>This is exercise 4 with time as <span class="m"><i>X</i></span> and before/after as the groups:</p>
      <ul class="cells">
        <li>Before: <span class="m"><i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>t</i> = 20 + 2<i>t</i></span></li>
        <li>After: <span class="m"><i>Y</i> = (<i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub>) + (<i>β</i><sub>1</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub>)<i>t</i> = 30 + 5<i>t</i></span></li>
      </ul>
      <p>Because <span class="m"><i>t</i><sub>after</sub> = 0</span> at the first post period, the two lines
        differ by exactly <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></span> at <span class="m"><i>t</i> = 0</span>.
        That is the gap between the observed post level (30) and where the old trend would have been (20).
        <strong>Centering time at the interruption is what makes the dummy coefficient mean
        &ldquo;jump at the interruption.&rdquo;</strong> Note that <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>0</sub> = 20</span>
        is not an observed point; it is the pre-trend extrapolated to <span class="m"><i>t</i> = 0</span>, the
        counterfactual level.</p>

      <h4>Design matrix</h4>
      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="dm">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Observation type</th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>Y</i></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m">1</span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>t</i></span></th><th scope="col" class="off"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>pre</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>t</i><sub>after</sub></span></th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><th scope="row">Before, <span class="m"><i>t</i> = &minus;2</span></th><td class="y">16</td><td>1</td><td>&minus;2</td><td class="off">1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Before, <span class="m"><i>t</i> = &minus;1</span></th><td class="y">18</td><td>1</td><td>&minus;1</td><td class="off">1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">First post, <span class="m"><i>t</i> = 0</span></th><td class="y">30</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td class="off">0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Post, <span class="m"><i>t</i> = 1</span></th><td class="y">35</td><td>1</td><td>1</td><td class="off">0</td><td>1</td><td>1</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="coef">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Coefficient</th><th scope="col">Value</th><th scope="col">Testing it equals zero asks&hellip;</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">Pre-period reference</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>20</td><td>Is the extrapolated pre level at <span class="m"><i>t</i> = 0</span> zero? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>2</td><td>Was there a pre-intervention trend?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></td><td>10</td><td>Was there an immediate level change at the interruption?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>3</sub></td><td>3</td><td>Did the slope change after the interruption?</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="mistake">
        <span class="lbl">Common mistakes</span>
        <ul>
          <li><strong>Using only <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span> to test a slope change.</strong> A
            dummy on its own gives a jump with parallel lines.</li>
          <li><strong>Starting the post-period counter at 1.</strong> If
            <span class="m"><i>t</i><sub>after</sub> = 1</span> in the first post period, the post line becomes
            <span class="m">(<i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub>) + (<i>β</i><sub>1</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub>)<i>t</i></span>.
            The jump at <span class="m"><i>t</i> = 0</span> is then <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub></span>,
            and <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></span> alone (here 7, not 10) is a gap one period
            <em>before</em> the interruption.</li>
          <li><strong>Adding <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>pre</sub></span> alongside
            <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span> and the intercept.</strong> Use one or the other.</li>
        </ul>
      </div>
      <a class="to-sol" href="#q8">&larr; Back to question</a>
    </article>

    <!-- 9 ------------------------------------------------------------- -->
    <article class="ex" id="s9">
      <h3>9. Regression discontinuity at a cutoff</h3>
      <figure class="fig">
```

```{r s09, fig.alt="Outcome against running variable minus cutoff: the line below reaches 40 at the cutoff, the line above starts at 50 and is steeper."}
fig_09()
```

```{=html}
      </figure>
      <div class="prompt"><p>An eligibility rule switches on at running-variable value
        <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 50</span>. The expected outcome jumps by 10 at the cutoff, and the two local
        slopes differ. Code the running variable and threshold dummy so the jump is one coefficient. Why
        center at 50?</p></div>

      <div class="callout">
        <span class="lbl">Short answer</span>
        <p>Let <span class="m"><i>x</i><sub>c</sub> = <i>X</i> &minus; 50</span> and
          <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>above</sub> = I(<i>X</i> &ge; 50)</span>. Then
          <span class="m"><i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>x</i><sub>c</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub><i>d</i><sub>above</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub>(<i>x</i><sub>c</sub><i>d</i><sub>above</sub>) + <i>ε</i></span>
          gives <span class="m">(40, 2, 10, 2)</span>, and <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></span> is the jump
          at the cutoff. Center at 50 because, in a model with an interaction, the dummy measures the gap where
          the running variable equals zero. Centering puts zero at the cutoff.</p>
      </div>

      <h4>Why this works</h4>
      <p>This is exercise 8 again, with the running variable in place of time:</p>
      <ul class="cells">
        <li>Below: <span class="m"><i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>x</i><sub>c</sub> = 40 + 2<i>x</i><sub>c</sub></span></li>
        <li>Above: <span class="m"><i>Y</i> = (<i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub>) + (<i>β</i><sub>1</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub>)<i>x</i><sub>c</sub> = 50 + 4<i>x</i><sub>c</sub></span></li>
      </ul>
      <p>At the cutoff, <span class="m"><i>x</i><sub>c</sub> = 0</span> and the lines differ by
        <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></span>. The value 40 is a <strong>left-hand limit</strong>: where the
        untreated line would arrive at the cutoff. Nobody at <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 50</span> is untreated,
        so it is never observed directly.</p>
      <p>To see why centering matters, fit the same lines with raw <span class="m"><i>X</i></span>. The lines
        become <span class="m">&minus;60 + 2<i>X</i></span> and <span class="m">&minus;150 + 4<i>X</i></span>, so the
        dummy coefficient is <span class="m">&minus;90</span>: the gap between two lines extrapolated all the way
        to <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 0</span>, far outside the data. The jump at 50 is still there, but only as
        <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub> + 50<i>β</i><sub>3</sub> = &minus;90 + 100 = 10</span>.</p>

      <h4>Design matrix</h4>
      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="dm">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Observation type</th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>Y</i></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m">1</span></th><th scope="col" class="off"><span class="m"><i>X</i></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>x</i><sub>c</sub></span></th><th scope="col" class="off"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>below</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>above</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>x</i><sub>c</sub><i>d</i><sub>above</sub></span></th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><th scope="row">Below, <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 48</span></th><td class="y">36</td><td>1</td><td class="off">48</td><td>&minus;2</td><td class="off">1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Below, <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 49</span></th><td class="y">38</td><td>1</td><td class="off">49</td><td>&minus;1</td><td class="off">1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Cutoff, <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 50</span></th><td class="y">50</td><td>1</td><td class="off">50</td><td>0</td><td class="off">0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Above, <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 51</span></th><td class="y">54</td><td>1</td><td class="off">51</td><td>1</td><td class="off">0</td><td>1</td><td>1</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>
      <p>Raw <span class="m"><i>X</i></span> is shown only to explain centering. Including both
        <span class="m"><i>X</i></span> and <span class="m"><i>x</i><sub>c</sub></span> with an intercept is
        collinear. Using <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>below</sub></span> instead of
        <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>above</sub></span> reverses the sign of the jump.</p>

      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="coef">
```
