          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Coefficient</th><th scope="col">Value</th><th scope="col">Testing it equals zero asks&hellip;</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">Below-cutoff reference</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>40</td><td>Is the left-hand limit at the cutoff zero? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>2</td><td>Is there a slope below the cutoff?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></td><td>10</td><td>Is there a jump at the cutoff?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>3</sub></td><td>2</td><td>Do the slopes differ above and below the cutoff?</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="mistake">
        <span class="lbl">Common mistakes</span>
        <ul>
          <li><strong>Interacting raw <span class="m"><i>X</i></span> with
            <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>above</sub></span> and calling the dummy coefficient the jump.</strong> As
            shown above, that coefficient is the gap at <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 0</span> (&minus;90), not at
            the cutoff.</li>
          <li><strong>Fitting one global line to all the data.</strong> RD identifies an effect only near the
            cutoff. Observations far from 50 say little about the jump, and a straight line through them can
            invent or hide one.</li>
        </ul>
      </div>
      <a class="to-sol" href="#q9">&larr; Back to question</a>
    </article>

    <!-- 10 ------------------------------------------------------------ -->
    <article class="ex" id="s10">
      <h3>10. A special pile of observations at predictor zero</h3>
      <figure class="fig">
```

```{r s10, fig.alt="Donations rise with fundraising expense along the line 10 + 4X; organizations with zero expense cluster around 30."}
fig_10()
```

```{=html}
      </figure>
      <div class="prompt"><p>Among organizations with positive fundraising expense <span class="m"><i>X</i></span>,
        donations follow approximately <span class="m">10 + 4<i>X</i></span>. Organizations with
        <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 0</span> have mean donations of 30. Add a dummy that tests whether the zero
        cases follow the extrapolated positive-<span class="m"><i>X</i></span> line. Which value of the line is
        the comparison?</p></div>

      <div class="callout">
        <span class="lbl">Short answer</span>
        <p>Add <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>zero</sub> = I(<i>X</i> = 0)</span>:
          <span class="m"><i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>X</i> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub><i>d</i><sub>zero</sub> + <i>ε</i></span>
          gives <span class="m">(10, 4, 20)</span>. <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></span> compares the
          zero group&rsquo;s mean (30) with the <strong>positive-case line extrapolated to
          <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 0</span></strong> (10). It is not a comparison with the average positive
          organization.</p>
      </div>

      <h4>Why this works</h4>
      <ul class="cells">
        <li>Zero cases (<span class="m"><i>X</i> = 0</span>, <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>zero</sub> = 1</span>): <span class="m"><i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub> = 30</span></li>
        <li>Positive cases (<span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>zero</sub> = 0</span>): <span class="m"><i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>X</i> = 10 + 4<i>X</i></span></li>
      </ul>
      <p>The zero group gets its own mean through <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub></span>,
        so the line (<span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>0</sub></span> and <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></span>)
        is estimated from the positive cases alone. That is the second benefit of the dummy. Without it, the pile
        at 30 would drag the intercept up and flatten the slope, misdescribing the organizations that do
        fundraise. <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></span> asks whether &ldquo;zero&rdquo; behaves like the
        smallest possible amount of fundraising, or like a different kind of organization. Here it is clearly
        the second: non-fundraisers raise far more than the line predicts.</p>

      <h4>Design matrix</h4>
      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="dm">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Observation type</th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>Y</i></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m">1</span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>X</i></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>zero</sub></span></th><th scope="col" class="off"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>positive</sub></span></th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><th scope="row">Zero expense</th><td class="y">30</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td class="off">0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Positive, <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 2</span></th><td class="y">18</td><td>1</td><td>2</td><td>0</td><td class="off">1</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Positive, <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 5</span></th><td class="y">30</td><td>1</td><td>5</td><td>0</td><td class="off">1</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <h4>Models</h4>
      <div class="eq"><span class="m">Zero indicator: <i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>X</i> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub><i>d</i><sub>zero</sub> + <i>ε</i></span></div>
      <div class="eq"><span class="m">Positive indicator: <i>Y</i> = <i>γ</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>γ</i><sub>1</sub><i>X</i> + <i>γ</i><sub>2</sub><i>d</i><sub>positive</sub> + <i>ε</i></span></div>

      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="coef">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Coefficient</th><th scope="col">Value</th><th scope="col">Testing it equals zero asks&hellip;</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">Zero indicator</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>10</td><td>Is the positive-case line zero at <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 0</span>? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>4</td><td>Do donations rise with fundraising among positive cases?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></td><td>20</td><td>Do zero cases sit on the extrapolated line?</td></tr>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">Positive indicator</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>30</td><td>Is the zero-group mean zero? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>4</td><td>Do donations rise with fundraising among positive cases?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>2</sub></td><td>&minus;20</td><td>Does the extrapolated line meet the zero-group mean at <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 0</span>?</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="mistake">
        <span class="lbl">Common mistakes</span>
        <ul>
          <li><strong>Putting <span class="m">I(<i>Y</i> = 0)</span> on the right-hand side.</strong> The pile-up
            is in <span class="m"><i>X</i></span>, not <span class="m"><i>Y</i></span>, and a predictor built from
            the outcome is never legitimate.</li>
          <li><strong>Reading <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></span> as &ldquo;zero cases versus the average
            positive case.&rdquo;</strong> It compares with the line at <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 0</span>.</li>
          <li><strong>Adding <span class="m"><i>X</i>&middot;<i>d</i><sub>zero</sub></span> for a zero-group
            slope.</strong> The column is always zero, since <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 0</span> whenever
            <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>zero</sub> = 1</span>. A group with one <span class="m"><i>X</i></span>
            value has no slope.</li>
        </ul>
      </div>
      <a class="to-sol" href="#q10">&larr; Back to question</a>
    </article>

    <!-- 11 ------------------------------------------------------------ -->
    <article class="ex" id="s11">
      <h3>11. Zero group and size-specific slopes</h3>
      <figure class="fig">
```

```{r s11, fig.alt="Zero-expense organizations cluster near 30; small organizations follow 10 + 3X; large organizations follow a steeper, higher line 17 + 5X."}
fig_11()
```

```{=html}
      </figure>
      <div class="prompt"><p>The zero-<span class="m"><i>X</i></span> cases have a distinct mean. Among
        positive-<span class="m"><i>X</i></span> cases, large organizations have a different intercept and slope
        from small ones. Specify the model so each of these three departures is a coefficient. How must size
        be coded for the zero cases?</p></div>

      <div class="callout">
        <span class="lbl">Short answer</span>
        <p>With small positive-<span class="m"><i>X</i></span> organizations as the reference,
          <span class="m"><i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>X</i> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub><i>d</i><sub>zero</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub><i>d</i><sub>large</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>4</sub>(<i>X</i><i>d</i><sub>large</sub>) + <i>ε</i></span>
          gives <span class="m">(10, 3, 20, 7, 2)</span>. The three departures are
          <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></span> (zero group), <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>3</sub></span>
          (large intercept), and <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>4</sub></span> (large slope). Code
          <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>large</sub> = 0</span> for every zero case, so the zero group is a third
          category rather than a subset of small or large.</p>
      </div>

      <h4>Why this works</h4>
      <p>The model describes three groups, each with its own equation:</p>
      <ul class="cells">
        <li>Zero cases: <span class="m"><i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub> = 30</span></li>
        <li>Small, positive: <span class="m"><i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>X</i> = 10 + 3<i>X</i></span></li>
        <li>Large, positive: <span class="m"><i>Y</i> = (<i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub>) + (<i>β</i><sub>1</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>4</sub>)<i>X</i> = 17 + 5<i>X</i></span></li>
      </ul>
      <p>This combines exercise 10 (a dummy for the pile at zero) with exercise 4 (intercept and slope shifts
        for a second group). The coding of size for zero cases matters. If a large zero-expense organization
        had <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>large</sub> = 1</span>, its prediction would be
        <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub></span>. Then
        <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>3</sub></span> would have to describe both the gap between the positive
        lines <em>and</em> a size gap within the zero group, forcing the two to be equal.</p>
      <p>If size genuinely matters among zero cases, code it for them and add
        <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>zero</sub><i>d</i><sub>large</sub></span>, so the zero group can have
        separate small and large means.</p>

      <h4>Design matrix</h4>
      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="dm">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Observation type</th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>Y</i></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m">1</span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>X</i></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>zero</sub></span></th><th scope="col" class="off"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>small</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>large</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>X</i><i>d</i><sub>large</sub></span></th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><th scope="row">Zero <span class="m"><i>X</i></span></th><td class="y">30</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td class="off">0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Small, <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 2</span></th><td class="y">16</td><td>1</td><td>2</td><td>0</td><td class="off">1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Small, <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 5</span></th><td class="y">25</td><td>1</td><td>5</td><td>0</td><td class="off">1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Large, <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 2</span></th><td class="y">27</td><td>1</td><td>2</td><td>0</td><td class="off">0</td><td>1</td><td>2</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Large, <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 5</span></th><td class="y">42</td><td>1</td><td>5</td><td>0</td><td class="off">0</td><td>1</td><td>5</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="coef">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Coefficient</th><th scope="col">Value</th><th scope="col">Testing it equals zero asks&hellip;</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">Small-positive reference</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>10</td><td>Is the small-positive line zero at <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 0</span>? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>3</td><td>Do donations rise with fundraising for small organizations?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></td><td>20</td><td>Do zero cases sit on the extrapolated small-organization line?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>3</sub></td><td>7</td><td>Do large and small lines meet at <span class="m"><i>X</i> = 0</span>?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>4</sub></td><td>2</td><td>Do large and small organizations have the same slope?</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="mistake">
        <span class="lbl">Common mistakes</span>
        <ul>
          <li><strong>Adding <span class="m"><i>X</i><i>d</i><sub>zero</sub></span> to give the zero group a
            slope.</strong> The column is all zeros.</li>
          <li><strong>Adding <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>small</sub></span> to the model.</strong>
            <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>zero</sub></span>, <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>small</sub></span>, and
            <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>large</sub></span> cover every case exactly once, so all three plus the
            intercept are collinear.</li>
        </ul>
      </div>
      <a class="to-sol" href="#q11">&larr; Back to question</a>
    </article>

    <!-- 12 ------------------------------------------------------------ -->
    <article class="ex" id="s12">
      <h3>12. A single outlying year</h3>
      <figure class="fig wide">
```

```{r s12, fig.width=7.5, fig.alt="Two panels of eleven yearly observations from 2010 to 2020 that rise one unit per year. In panel A the 2015 value is 10 units too high and the OLS line is lifted but keeps its slope. In panel B the 2020 value is 10 units too high and the OLS line is tilted upward."}
fig_12()
```

```{=html}
      </figure>
      <div class="prompt"><p>An outcome follows <span class="m"><i>Y</i> = <i>t</i></span>, with
        <span class="m"><i>t</i> = year &minus; 2009</span>, except that one year is 10 units too high: 2015 in
        panel A, 2020 in panel B. How does the odd year distort each OLS fit, and why differently? Add a
        <strong>single</strong> dummy that removes its influence. What does the dummy&rsquo;s coefficient
        measure, and what happens to the trend estimates?</p></div>

      <div class="callout">
        <span class="lbl">Short answer</span>
        <p>Without a dummy, the middle-year outlier (A) lifts the whole line but leaves the slope at 1.00. The
          last-year outlier (B) tilts the line, raising the slope to 1.45. Add a dummy that equals 1 in the odd
          year only, <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>2015</sub></span> or <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>2020</sub></span>:</p>
        <p><span class="m"><i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>t</i> + <i>δ</i><i>d</i><sub>odd</sub> + <i>ε</i></span></p>
        <p>In both panels this gives <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>0</sub> = 0</span>,
          <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>1</sub> = 1</span>, <span class="m"><i>δ</i> = 10</span>. The trend is
          estimated from the ten ordinary years, and <span class="m"><i>δ</i></span> is how far the odd year sits
          above that trend.</p>
      </div>

      <h4>How one point moves a line</h4>
      <p>An outlier pulls on the fitted line in two ways. It always raises the mean of
        <span class="m"><i>Y</i></span>, and the line must pass through
        <span class="m">(<i>t̄</i>, <i>Ȳ</i>)</span>, so the whole line lifts. How much it also <em>tilts</em> the
        line depends on its distance from the middle of the <span class="m"><i>t</i></span> values, its
        <strong>leverage</strong>:</p>
      <div class="eq"><span class="m">change in slope = 10 &times; (<i>t</i><sub>odd</sub> &minus; <i>t̄</i>) / &Sigma;(<i>t</i> &minus; <i>t̄</i>)<sup>2</sup> = 10 &times; (<i>t</i><sub>odd</sub> &minus; 6) / 110</span></div>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>Panel A, 2015</strong> (<span class="m"><i>t</i> = 6 = <i>t̄</i></span>): no leverage, so the
          slope stays at 1.00. The intercept rises from 0 to <span class="m">10/11 &asymp; 0.91</span>. The
          residuals balloon, so the slope&rsquo;s standard error jumps from about 0 to 0.30.</li>
        <li><strong>Panel B, 2020</strong> (<span class="m"><i>t</i> = 11</span>): maximum leverage. The slope
          rises by <span class="m">50/110 &asymp; 0.45</span> to 1.45, and the intercept falls to &minus;1.82 to
          compensate. An odd <em>first</em> year would do the opposite: slope 0.55, intercept 3.64.</li>
      </ul>
      <p>So a single bad year at the end of a series can manufacture or hide a trend, which is exactly where
        policy series tend to have their surprises.</p>

      <h4>Why one dummy fixes it</h4>
      <p>A dummy that is 1 for a single observation gives that observation its own intercept. The model can then
        fit it exactly (<span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>t</i> + <i>δ</i> = <i>Y</i></span>),
        so it has no residual left to pull the line with. The trend is estimated from the other ten years alone.
        That gives the same slope and intercept as deleting the year, but the observation stays in the data and
        you get a coefficient for it.</p>
      <p><span class="m"><i>δ</i></span> is the gap between the odd year and the value the trend predicts for
        it: <span class="m">16 &minus; 6 = 10</span> in panel A and <span class="m">21 &minus; 11 = 10</span> in
        panel B. Its t-test is the standard regression test for an outlier: is this year further from the trend
        than ordinary noise would put it?</p>

      <h4>Design matrix</h4>
      <p>Each panel uses only its own dummy.</p>
      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="dm">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Observation type</th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>Y</i></span> (A)</th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>Y</i></span> (B)</th><th scope="col"><span class="m">1</span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>t</i></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>2015</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>2020</sub></span></th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><th scope="row">2010</th><td class="y">1</td><td class="y">1</td><td>1</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">2014</th><td class="y">5</td><td class="y">5</td><td>1</td><td>5</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">2015</th><td class="y">16</td><td class="y">6</td><td>1</td><td>6</td><td>1</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">2016</th><td class="y">7</td><td class="y">7</td><td>1</td><td>7</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">2019</th><td class="y">10</td><td class="y">10</td><td>1</td><td>10</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">2020</th><td class="y">11</td><td class="y">21</td><td>1</td><td>11</td><td>0</td><td>1</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="coef">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Coefficient</th><th scope="col">Value</th><th scope="col">Testing it equals zero asks&hellip;</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">No dummy &middot; panel A / panel B</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>0.91 / &minus;1.82</td><td>Is the fitted line zero at <span class="m"><i>t</i> = 0</span>? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>1.00 / 1.45</td><td>Is there a trend? (A is right but noisy; B is biased by the endpoint)</td></tr>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">With the odd-year dummy &middot; both panels</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>0</td><td>Is the trend zero at <span class="m"><i>t</i> = 0</span>? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>1</td><td>Is there a trend among the ordinary years?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>δ</i></td><td>10</td><td>Does the odd year sit on the trend line?</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="mistake">
        <span class="lbl">Common mistakes</span>
        <ul>
          <li><strong>Deleting the year without saying so.</strong> The line is the same, but readers cannot see
            the decision and you lose the test of whether the year really was unusual.</li>
          <li><strong>Adding a dummy for every point that does not fit.</strong> A dummy should have a reason
            that exists before you look at the residuals: a known strike, a coding change, a pandemic. Give
            enough points their own dummy and any line fits perfectly.</li>
          <li><strong>Reading the dummy&rsquo;s p-value at face value after hunting for the biggest
            residual.</strong> Picking the worst of eleven years and then testing it is eleven tests, not one. The
            multiple-comparison logic of the Bonferroni correction (Unit 09) applies.</li>
          <li><strong>Using a step dummy (1 from 2015 onward) for a one-year blip.</strong> That models a
            permanent shift, not a single odd year.</li>
        </ul>
      </div>
      <a class="to-sol" href="#q12">&larr; Back to question</a>
    </article>

    <!-- 13A ----------------------------------------------------------- -->
    <article class="ex" id="s13a">
      <h3>13A. Flat before, flat after</h3>
      <figure class="fig wide">
```

```{r s13a, fig.width=7.5, fig.alt="The outcome is flat at 60 from 2014 to 2019, falls to 44, 42, and 53 in 2020 to 2022, and is flat at 60 again from 2023 to 2027."}
fig_13a()
```

```{=html}
      </figure>
      <div class="prompt"><p>The outcome is flat at 60 before COVID (2014&ndash;2019), drops to 44, 42, and 53 in
        2020&ndash;2022, and is flat at 60 again afterwards (2023&ndash;2027). Build a model that (a) gives each
        anomalous year its own deviation and (b) tests whether the post-COVID level differs from the pre-COVID
        level. Which category is omitted, and what is the post contrast? What goes wrong if the COVID years are
        left in the reference group instead?</p></div>

      <div class="callout">
        <span class="lbl">Short answer</span>
        <p>Omit <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>pre</sub></span>:</p>
        <p><span class="m"><i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>δ</i><sub>20</sub><i>d</i><sub>covid20</sub> + <i>δ</i><sub>21</sub><i>d</i><sub>covid21</sub> + <i>δ</i><sub>22</sub><i>d</i><sub>covid22</sub> + <i>δ</i><sub>P</sub><i>d</i><sub>post</sub> + <i>ε</i></span></p>
        <p>This gives <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>0</sub> = 60</span>, anomaly deviations
          <span class="m">(&minus;16, &minus;18, &minus;7)</span>, and <span class="m"><i>δ</i><sub>P</sub> = 0</span>:
          the outcome went back to exactly where it was. If the COVID years are left in the reference group, the
          same data show a spurious post-COVID <em>gain</em> of about 4.6.</p>
      </div>

      <h4>Why this works</h4>
      <p>This is exercise 12 three times over. Each anomaly year has its own dummy, so each is fit exactly and
        cannot contaminate either the pre or the post level. With no trend in the model, every coefficient is a
        plain difference in means from the pre-COVID years:</p>
      <ul class="cells">
        <li>Pre years: <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>0</sub> = 60</span></li>
        <li>2020: <span class="m">60 + <i>δ</i><sub>20</sub> = 44 &rarr; <i>δ</i><sub>20</sub> = &minus;16</span>;
          2021: <span class="m"><i>δ</i><sub>21</sub> = &minus;18</span>; 2022: <span class="m"><i>δ</i><sub>22</sub> = &minus;7</span></li>
        <li>Post years: <span class="m">60 + <i>δ</i><sub>P</sub> = 60 &rarr; <i>δ</i><sub>P</sub> = 0</span></li>
      </ul>
      <p>Because nothing else changes over time, <span class="m"><i>δ</i><sub>P</sub></span> here <em>is</em> the
        raw difference between the post and pre means, and that is the right contrast. Keep this in mind for
        13B, where adding a trend breaks that equivalence.</p>
      <p>Two separate questions, two separate tests. Was there a temporary disruption? Test
        <span class="m"><i>δ</i><sub>20</sub> = <i>δ</i><sub>21</sub> = <i>δ</i><sub>22</sub> = 0</span> jointly.
        Is there a lasting change? Test <span class="m"><i>δ</i><sub>P</sub> = 0</span>. Here the answers are
        yes and no.</p>

      <h4>What goes wrong without the COVID dummies</h4>
      <p>The anomaly years have to go <em>somewhere</em>. If you code only
        <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span>, they join whichever group is left:</p>
      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="coef">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">COVID years placed in&hellip;</th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>δ</i><sub>P</sub></span></th><th scope="col">What the model concludes</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><td>their own dummies</td><td>0</td><td>No lasting change. Correct.</td></tr>
            <tr><td>the reference (pre) group</td><td>+4.6</td><td>The pre mean drops to <span class="m">(6&middot;60 + 44 + 42 + 53)/9 &asymp; 55.4</span>, so post looks like a gain.</td></tr>
            <tr><td>the post group</td><td>&minus;5.1</td><td>The post mean drops to <span class="m">(44 + 42 + 53 + 5&middot;60)/8 &asymp; 54.9</span>, so post looks like a loss.</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>
      <p>The same three odd years produce a gain, a loss, or nothing, depending only on where they are filed.
        That is exercise 12&rsquo;s lesson about a single outlier, in dummy-variable form.</p>

      <h4>Design matrix</h4>
      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="dm">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Observation type</th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>Y</i></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m">1</span></th><th scope="col" class="off"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>pre</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>covid20</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>covid21</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>covid22</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span></th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><th scope="row">Pre, 2014</th><td class="y">60</td><td>1</td><td class="off">1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Pre, 2019</th><td class="y">60</td><td>1</td><td class="off">1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">COVID, 2020</th><td class="y">44</td><td>1</td><td class="off">0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">COVID, 2021</th><td class="y">42</td><td>1</td><td class="off">0</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">COVID, 2022</th><td class="y">53</td><td>1</td><td class="off">0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Post, 2023</th><td class="y">60</td><td>1</td><td class="off">0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>1</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Post, 2027</th><td class="y">60</td><td>1</td><td class="off">0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>1</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>
      <p>In the shorthand <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>0</sub>, &hellip;, <i>d</i><sub>4</sub></span>, these five
        indicators are <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>pre</sub>, <i>d</i><sub>covid20</sub>, <i>d</i><sub>covid21</sub>,
        <i>d</i><sub>covid22</sub>, <i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span> in that order.</p>

      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="coef">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Coefficient</th><th scope="col">Value</th><th scope="col">Testing it equals zero asks&hellip;</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">Pre-COVID reference</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>60</td><td>Is the pre-COVID level zero? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>δ</i><sub>20</sub></td><td>&minus;16</td><td>Was 2020 at the pre-COVID level?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>δ</i><sub>21</sub></td><td>&minus;18</td><td>Was 2021 at the pre-COVID level?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>δ</i><sub>22</sub></td><td>&minus;7</td><td>Was 2022 at the pre-COVID level?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>δ</i><sub>P</sub></td><td>0</td><td>Is the post-COVID level different from the pre-COVID level?</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="mistake">
        <span class="lbl">Common mistakes</span>
        <ul>
          <li><strong>Coding only <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span>.</strong> The COVID years land in
            one of the comparison groups and create a shift that is not there (table above).</li>
          <li><strong>Using one <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>covid</sub></span> dummy for all three
            years.</strong> That protects the pre and post levels, but forces 2020&ndash;2022 to share one mean
            and hides the recovery path (&minus;16, &minus;18, &minus;7).</li>
          <li><strong>Including all five period dummies with the intercept.</strong> They sum to one on every
            row.</li>
        </ul>
      </div>
      <a class="to-sol" href="#q13a">&larr; Back to question</a>
    </article>

    <!-- 13B ----------------------------------------------------------- -->
    <article class="ex" id="s13b">
      <h3>13B. Add a trend</h3>
      <figure class="fig wide">
```

```{r s13b, fig.width=7.5, fig.alt="A pre-COVID trend from 50 in 2014 rising 2 per year; anomalous low values in 2020 to 2022; a stable post period from 2023 that runs parallel to the extrapolated trend but 9 units above it."}
fig_13b()
```

```{=html}
      </figure>
      <div class="prompt"><p>Same indicators as 13A, but now the outcome rises 2 units per year before COVID, and
        the later line is parallel to the pretrend but 9 units above it. Build a model that (a) gives each
        anomalous year its own deviation and (b) tests whether the later regime is at a new level relative to
        the pre-COVID trend <strong>at the same calendar time</strong>. Which category is omitted? Is the
        <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span> coefficient still an unadjusted difference in period
        means, as it was in 13A?</p></div>

      <div class="callout">
        <span class="lbl">Short answer</span>
        <p>Keep the 13A dummies, still omitting <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>pre</sub></span>, and add a calendar
          trend <span class="m"><i>t</i> = year &minus; 2014</span>:</p>
        <p><span class="m"><i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>t</i> + <i>δ</i><sub>20</sub><i>d</i><sub>covid20</sub> + <i>δ</i><sub>21</sub><i>d</i><sub>covid21</sub> + <i>δ</i><sub>22</sub><i>d</i><sub>covid22</sub> + <i>δ</i><sub>P</sub><i>d</i><sub>post</sub> + <i>ε</i></span></p>
        <p>This gives a trend of <span class="m">50 + 2<i>t</i></span>, anomaly deviations
          <span class="m">(&minus;18, &minus;22, &minus;13)</span>, and <span class="m"><i>δ</i><sub>P</sub> = 9</span>.
          <strong>No</strong>, unlike 13A, <span class="m"><i>δ</i><sub>P</sub></span> is no longer the raw
          difference in period means. That raw difference is 26, and 17 of it is just the old trend
          continuing.</p>
      </div>

      <h4>Why this works</h4>
      <p>Because the trend term is in the model, every dummy coefficient is a <em>vertical</em> distance from the
        pre-COVID trend line, measured in the same year. Omitting <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>pre</sub></span>
        makes the ordinary pre years the reference, so the trend line is estimated from them. In 13A the
        reference line was flat, so &ldquo;distance from the line&rdquo; and &ldquo;difference in means&rdquo;
        were the same thing. Here they are not.</p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>Each anomaly year gets its own dummy.</strong> As in exercise 12, one dummy for a single year
          fits that year exactly, so the three unusual points cannot pull the trend line around. Each
          <span class="m"><i>δ</i></span> is that year&rsquo;s deviation from where the trend would have put it.
          For 2020, the trend predicts <span class="m">50 + 2&middot;6 = 62</span> and the observed value is 44,
          so <span class="m"><i>δ</i><sub>20</sub> = &minus;18</span>.</li>
        <li><strong><span class="m"><i>δ</i><sub>P</sub></span> is a shift, not a change in means.</strong> In
          2023 the trend predicts <span class="m">50 + 2&middot;9 = 68</span> and the observed value is 77, a gap
          of 9. Because the post line is parallel, the gap is 9 in every post year.</li>
      </ul>
      <p>Compare that with the naive comparison. The post-period mean (2023&ndash;2027) is 81 and the pre-period
        mean (2014&ndash;2019) is 55, a difference of 26. But the trend alone would have raised the mean from 55 to
        72 across those years (+17). Only the remaining 9 is a new level.</p>
      <p>To test for a temporary disruption, test the three anomaly coefficients <em>jointly</em>:
        <span class="m"><i>δ</i><sub>20</sub> = <i>δ</i><sub>21</sub> = <i>δ</i><sub>22</sub> = 0</span> (an
        F-test). To test for a lasting shift, test <span class="m"><i>δ</i><sub>P</sub> = 0</span>.</p>

      <h4>Design matrix</h4>
      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="dm">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Observation type</th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>Y</i></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m">1</span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>t</i></span></th><th scope="col" class="off"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>pre</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>covid20</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>covid21</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>covid22</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span></th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><th scope="row">Pre, 2014</th><td class="y">50</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td class="off">1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Pre, 2019</th><td class="y">60</td><td>1</td><td>5</td><td class="off">1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">COVID, 2020</th><td class="y">44</td><td>1</td><td>6</td><td class="off">0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">COVID, 2021</th><td class="y">42</td><td>1</td><td>7</td><td class="off">0</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">COVID, 2022</th><td class="y">53</td><td>1</td><td>8</td><td class="off">0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Post, 2023</th><td class="y">77</td><td>1</td><td>9</td><td class="off">0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>1</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Post, 2025</th><td class="y">81</td><td>1</td><td>11</td><td class="off">0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>1</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>
      <p>In the shorthand <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>0</sub>, &hellip;, <i>d</i><sub>4</sub></span>, these five
        indicators are <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>pre</sub>, <i>d</i><sub>covid20</sub>, <i>d</i><sub>covid21</sub>,
        <i>d</i><sub>covid22</sub>, <i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span> in that order.</p>

      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="coef">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Coefficient</th><th scope="col">Value</th><th scope="col">Testing it equals zero asks&hellip;</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">Pre-COVID reference</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>50</td><td>Is the trend level in 2014 zero? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>2</td><td>Was there a pre-COVID trend?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>δ</i><sub>20</sub></td><td>&minus;18</td><td>Was 2020 on the extrapolated trend?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>δ</i><sub>21</sub></td><td>&minus;22</td><td>Was 2021 on the extrapolated trend?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>δ</i><sub>22</sub></td><td>&minus;13</td><td>Was 2022 on the extrapolated trend?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>δ</i><sub>P</sub></td><td>9</td><td>Is the stable post period on the extrapolated trend, compared in the same year?</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="mistake">
        <span class="lbl">Common mistakes</span>
        <ul>
          <li><strong>Regressing on <span class="m">1</span> and <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span>
            alone.</strong> This compares raw means from different years (26) and credits the ordinary trend to
            the new regime.</li>
          <li><strong>Including all five period dummies with the intercept.</strong> They sum to one on every
            row.</li>
          <li><strong>Reading <span class="m"><i>δ</i><sub>P</sub></span> as the effect of COVID.</strong> It shows
            that the level shifted around 2023. Attributing the shift to COVID needs a design argument (a
            comparison series, a mechanism), not just the coefficient.</li>
        </ul>
      </div>
      <a class="to-sol" href="#q13b">&larr; Back to question</a>
    </article>

    <!-- 13C ----------------------------------------------------------- -->
    <article class="ex" id="s13c">
      <h3>13C. What if the post-COVID slope changed?</h3>
      <figure class="fig wide">
```

```{r s13c, fig.width=7.5, fig.alt="The same picture with an alternative red post-period line that starts at 77 in 2023 and rises 4 per year."}
fig_13c()
```

```{=html}
      </figure>
      <div class="prompt"><p>In the alternative red post period, the slope is 2 units per year steeper than
        before. Add one term that tests this change. Define time so that the post-level coefficient is still the
        vertical gap at the start of the stable post period. What is the post slope?</p></div>

      <div class="callout">
        <span class="lbl">Short answer</span>
        <p>Keep the model from 13B and add
          <span class="m"><i>t</i><sub>post</sub> = (year &minus; 2023)&middot;<i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span>,
          which is zero before 2023 <em>and</em> in 2023 itself. Its coefficient
          <span class="m"><i>θ</i> = 2</span> tests the slope change, <span class="m"><i>δ</i><sub>P</sub> = 9</span>
          is still the jump in 2023, and the post slope is
          <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>1</sub> + <i>θ</i> = 4</span>.</p>
      </div>

      <h4>Why this works</h4>
      <p>This is the interrupted time series of exercise 8 on top of the anomaly dummies of exercise 13B. The post
        line is</p>
      <div class="eq"><span class="m"><i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>t</i> + <i>δ</i><sub>P</sub> + <i>θ</i>(year &minus; 2023)</span></div>
      <p>In 2023 the last term vanishes, so the gap from the pretrend there is exactly
        <span class="m"><i>δ</i><sub>P</sub></span>. Each later year adds <span class="m"><i>θ</i></span> to the
        gap. Starting the post clock at 2023 is what keeps <span class="m"><i>δ</i><sub>P</sub></span> meaning
        &ldquo;the jump at the start of the new regime.&rdquo;</p>
      <p>Suppose you used <span class="m"><i>t</i>&middot;<i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span> instead, with
        <span class="m"><i>t</i></span> counted from 2014. The post line would then be
        <span class="m">(<i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>δ</i><sub>P</sub>) + (<i>β</i><sub>1</sub> + <i>θ</i>)<i>t</i></span>,
        so <span class="m"><i>δ</i><sub>P</sub></span> would be the gap extrapolated back to 2014:
        <span class="m">9 &minus; 9&middot;2 = &minus;9</span>. The fit is identical, but the sign of the headline
        coefficient flips.</p>
      <p>Test the two components separately, or test <span class="m"><i>δ</i><sub>P</sub> = <i>θ</i> = 0</span>
        jointly to ask whether the post regime differs from the old trend in any way.</p>

      <h4>Design matrix</h4>
      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="dm">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Observation type</th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>Y</i></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m">1</span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>t</i></span></th><th scope="col" class="off"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>pre</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>covid20</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>covid21</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>covid22</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>t</i><sub>post</sub></span></th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><th scope="row">Pre, 2014</th><td class="y">50</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td class="off">1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Pre, 2019</th><td class="y">60</td><td>1</td><td>5</td><td class="off">1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">COVID, 2020</th><td class="y">44</td><td>1</td><td>6</td><td class="off">0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">COVID, 2021</th><td class="y">42</td><td>1</td><td>7</td><td class="off">0</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">COVID, 2022</th><td class="y">53</td><td>1</td><td>8</td><td class="off">0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Post, 2023</th><td class="y">77</td><td>1</td><td>9</td><td class="off">0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Post, 2025</th><td class="y">85</td><td>1</td><td>11</td><td class="off">0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>2</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">Post, 2027</th><td class="y">93</td><td>1</td><td>13</td><td class="off">0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>4</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="coef">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Coefficient</th><th scope="col">Value</th><th scope="col">Testing it equals zero asks&hellip;</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">Pre-COVID reference</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>50</td><td>Is the trend level in 2014 zero? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>2</td><td>Was there a pre-COVID trend?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>δ</i><sub>20</sub>, <i>δ</i><sub>21</sub>, <i>δ</i><sub>22</sub></td><td>&minus;18, &minus;22, &minus;13</td><td>Was each anomaly year on the extrapolated trend?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>δ</i><sub>P</sub></td><td>9</td><td>Was 2023 on the extrapolated trend?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>θ</i></td><td>2</td><td>Is the post slope the same as the pre slope?</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="mistake">
        <span class="lbl">Common mistakes</span>
        <ul>
          <li><strong>Inferring a slope change from <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span> alone.</strong>
            That term shifts the level only.</li>
          <li><strong>Using raw <span class="m">year &times; <i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span> and reading
            <span class="m"><i>δ</i><sub>P</sub></span> as the gap in 2023.</strong> As shown above, it becomes a
            gap extrapolated to year zero of whatever clock you used. Center the post clock at 2023.</li>
        </ul>
      </div>
      <a class="to-sol" href="#q13c">&larr; Back to question</a>
    </article>

    <!-- 14 ------------------------------------------------------------ -->
    <article class="ex" id="s14">
      <h3>14. Reverse-engineer the coding</h3>
      <figure class="fig">
```

```{r s14, fig.alt="Group A rises from 50 to 55; group B rises from 50 to 70."}
fig_14()
```

```{=html}
      </figure>
      <div class="prompt"><p>Group A changes from 50 to 55; B changes from 50 to 70. For each request, choose the
        group and time references so a <em>single coefficient</em> tests it. You may write a different model for
        each. (a) B versus A in the pre period; (b) B versus A in the post period; (c) B&rsquo;s own
        pre-to-post change; (d) the difference in changes. Are any of these impossible to isolate as one
        coefficient under a saturated 2 &times; 2 coding?</p></div>

      <div class="callout">
        <span class="lbl">Short answer</span>
        <ul>
          <li><strong>(a)</strong> Reference A/pre: the <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>B</sub></span> coefficient,
            <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>1</sub> = 0</span>.</li>
          <li><strong>(b)</strong> Reference A/post: the <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>B</sub></span> coefficient,
            <span class="m"><i>γ</i><sub>1</sub> = 15</span>.</li>
          <li><strong>(c)</strong> Reference B/pre: the <span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span> coefficient,
            <span class="m"><i>λ</i><sub>2</sub> = 20</span>.</li>
          <li><strong>(d)</strong> Any reference: the interaction, <span class="m">&plusmn;15</span>.</li>
        </ul>
        <p>None of the four is impossible. What <em>is</em> impossible is getting all four from one model, or
          getting a diagonal contrast (such as B/post versus A/pre) as a single coefficient under any coding.</p>
      </div>

      <h4>Why this works</h4>
      <p>A saturated 2 &times; 2 model has an intercept and three coefficients, and every one of them is anchored
        at the reference cell:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>the <strong>group</strong> main effect compares the two groups <em>in the reference period</em>;</li>
        <li>the <strong>period</strong> main effect is the change over time <em>for the reference group</em>;</li>
        <li>the <strong>interaction</strong> is the difference in changes, which is the same contrast from every
          reference, up to sign.</li>
      </ul>
      <p>So to test a group gap in a particular period, make that period the reference. To test one group&rsquo;s
        change, make that group the reference. The diagonal contrast from the reference cell is always
        the sum of all three coefficients (for example, B/post versus A/pre is
        <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>1</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub> = 20</span> in Model 1).
        No choice of reference makes it a single coefficient, so it needs a linear-combination test.</p>

      <h4>Design matrix</h4>
      <p>Choose one group indicator and one period indicator for each model. Each interaction column is the
        product of the two indicators you chose.</p>
      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="dm">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Observation type</th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>Y</i></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m">1</span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>A</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>B</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>pre</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>B</sub><i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>B</sub><i>d</i><sub>pre</sub></span></th><th scope="col"><span class="m"><i>d</i><sub>A</sub><i>d</i><sub>post</sub></span></th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><th scope="row">A, pre</th><td class="y">50</td><td>1</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">B, pre</th><td class="y">50</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">A, post</th><td class="y">55</td><td>1</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>1</td></tr>
            <tr><th scope="row">B, post</th><td class="y">70</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <h4>Models</h4>
      <p>The models are numbered rather than lettered, so they are not confused with groups A and B.</p>
      <div class="eq"><span class="m">Model 1 (A/pre): <i>Y</i> = <i>β</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>1</sub><i>d</i><sub>B</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>2</sub><i>d</i><sub>post</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub>(<i>d</i><sub>B</sub><i>d</i><sub>post</sub>) + <i>ε</i></span></div>
      <div class="eq"><span class="m">Model 2 (A/post): <i>Y</i> = <i>γ</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>γ</i><sub>1</sub><i>d</i><sub>B</sub> + <i>γ</i><sub>2</sub><i>d</i><sub>pre</sub> + <i>γ</i><sub>3</sub>(<i>d</i><sub>B</sub><i>d</i><sub>pre</sub>) + <i>ε</i></span></div>
      <div class="eq"><span class="m">Model 3 (B/pre): <i>Y</i> = <i>λ</i><sub>0</sub> + <i>λ</i><sub>1</sub><i>d</i><sub>A</sub> + <i>λ</i><sub>2</sub><i>d</i><sub>post</sub> + <i>λ</i><sub>3</sub>(<i>d</i><sub>A</sub><i>d</i><sub>post</sub>) + <i>ε</i></span></div>

      <div class="table-scroll tight">
        <table class="coef">
          <thead><tr><th scope="col">Coefficient</th><th scope="col">Value</th><th scope="col">Testing it equals zero asks&hellip;</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">Model 1 &middot; A/pre reference</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>50</td><td>Is the A pre mean zero? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>0</td><td><strong>(a)</strong> Are B and A equal in the pre period?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></td><td>5</td><td>Did A change from pre to post?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>β</i><sub>3</sub></td><td>15</td><td><strong>(d)</strong> Did B and A change by the same amount?</td></tr>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">Model 2 &middot; A/post reference</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>55</td><td>Is the A post mean zero? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>15</td><td><strong>(b)</strong> Are B and A equal in the post period?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>2</sub></td><td>&minus;5</td><td>Are A&rsquo;s pre and post means equal?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>γ</i><sub>3</sub></td><td>&minus;15</td><td><strong>(d)</strong> Is the B&minus;A gap the same pre and post?</td></tr>
            <tr class="grp"><th colspan="3" scope="rowgroup">Model 3 &middot; B/pre reference</th></tr>
            <tr><td><i>λ</i><sub>0</sub></td><td>50</td><td>Is the B pre mean zero? (descriptive only)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>λ</i><sub>1</sub></td><td>0</td><td>Are A and B equal in the pre period?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>λ</i><sub>2</sub></td><td>20</td><td><strong>(c)</strong> Did B change from pre to post?</td></tr>
            <tr><td><i>λ</i><sub>3</sub></td><td>&minus;15</td><td><strong>(d)</strong> Did A and B change by the same amount?</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="mistake">
        <span class="lbl">Common mistakes</span>
        <ul>
          <li><strong>Keeping A/pre as the reference and calling <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>1</sub></span> the
            post-period gap, or <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub></span> B&rsquo;s change.</strong> They are the
            pre-period gap and A&rsquo;s change. For the others, switch the reference or test a sum
            (<span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>1</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub></span>,
            <span class="m"><i>β</i><sub>2</sub> + <i>β</i><sub>3</sub></span>).</li>
          <li><strong>Calling the interaction &ldquo;B&rsquo;s change.&rdquo;</strong> It is the
            <em>difference</em> between B&rsquo;s change and A&rsquo;s.</li>
        </ul>
      </div>
      <a class="to-sol" href="#q14">&larr; Back to question</a>
    </article>
  </section>

  <!-- ================================================================== -->
  <section id="synthesis">
    <div class="sec-head">
      <p class="num">Section four</p>
      <h2>Quick synthesis</h2>
      <p class="sub">Every exercise is the same move: choose the reference and the zero point so the contrast you
        want lands on one coefficient.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="table-scroll">
      <table class="synth">
        <thead><tr><th scope="col">Contrast in the picture</th><th scope="col">Coding choice</th><th scope="col">Coefficient or restriction</th></tr></thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr><th scope="row">Sample mean versus a benchmark</th><td>Center the outcome at the benchmark</td><td>Intercept = 0</td></tr>
          <tr><th scope="row">Group versus reference group</th><td>Omit the comparison group</td><td>Group dummy = 0</td></tr>
          <tr><th scope="row">Same people before and after</th><td>Person intercepts, or difference scores</td><td>Post dummy = 0</td></tr>
          <tr><th scope="row">Difference in slopes</th><td>Interact the group dummy with <span class="m"><i>X</i></span></td><td>Interaction = 0</td></tr>
          <tr><th scope="row">Effect in one particular setting</th><td>Make that setting the reference</td><td>Program main effect = 0</td></tr>
          <tr><th scope="row">Difference in changes</th><td>Group &times; post</td><td>Interaction = 0</td></tr>
          <tr><th scope="row">Increment from one more dose</th><td>Cumulative &ldquo;at least <span class="m"><i>k</i></span>&rdquo; dummies</td><td>Dose-<span class="m"><i>k</i></span> dummy = 0</td></tr>
          <tr><th scope="row">Immediate jump at a date or cutoff</th><td>Center the running variable there</td><td>Post / threshold dummy = 0</td></tr>
          <tr><th scope="row">Slope change at a date or cutoff</th><td>Centered running variable &times; post dummy</td><td>Interaction = 0</td></tr>
          <tr><th scope="row">One outlying observation</th><td>A dummy equal to 1 for that observation only</td><td>That dummy = 0 (an outlier test)</td></tr>
          <tr><th scope="row">Temporary anomalous periods</th><td>One indicator per anomalous period</td><td>Joint F-test of those dummies</td></tr>
          <tr><th scope="row">New regime after anomalies</th><td>Pre regime omitted, calendar trend included</td><td>Post dummy = 0, at a common time</td></tr>
          <tr><th scope="row">Distinct group at predictor zero</th><td><span class="m">I(<i>X</i> = 0)</span></td><td>Zero dummy = 0, versus the extrapolated line</td></tr>
        </tbody>
      </table>
    </div>

    <h3>What should be clear in my mind?</h3>
    <ol class="checklist">
      <li><strong>Name the reference before reading any coefficient.</strong> Every dummy coefficient is a gap
        from the omitted category.</li>
      <li><strong>Know where each gap is measured.</strong> In a model with an interaction, a dummy
        coefficient is the gap where the continuous variable equals zero. Center to move that point where
        you want it.</li>
      <li><strong>Recover any cell or line by adding coefficients.</strong> Write the equation for each row of
        the design matrix and solve from the reference outward.</li>
      <li><strong>Distinguish imposing from testing.</strong> Leaving out an interaction <em>assumes</em>
        parallel lines; including it lets you test them.</li>
      <li><strong>When a contrast is a sum of coefficients</strong>, either recode so it becomes one coefficient,
        or run a linear-combination test.</li>
      <li><strong>Never enter a complete set of complementary indicators alongside an intercept.</strong></li>
    </ol>

    <div class="callout">
      <span class="lbl">Instructor note</span>
      <p>The diagrams deliberately show conditional means without sampling uncertainty. Have students write the
        estimand and the model first, then give them an actual dataset to fit the model with standard errors
        appropriate to its design (clustered for repeated measures, robust for unequal variances, and so
        on).</p>
    </div>
  </section>
